speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: SiT ROBERT BORDEN: I was asked yesterday with regard to a report from Col. Sherwood, Chief Oommissiomeir of Do-

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
minion Police, on the fire which occurred on Thursday last. On the 4th instant Col. Sherwood handed me a report which I did not get in time to bring down on that day, and I have since asked him if he desired to supplement it in any way. He says that it contains all the information with regard to the fire that is available up to the present time. The memorandum is: Chief Commissioner of Police, Canada, Ottawa, February 4, 1916. Memorandum for the Right Honourable the Prime Minister of Canada.
Sergeant Carroll who was in charge of the police on duty at the House of Commons last night, reports that at about 8.45 p.m., fire was discovered in the reading room among papers lying on the shelf of the second reading desk from the House of Commons entrance. Constable Moore was the nearest officer on duty at that point and his attention was called to it by a gentleman whom he recognized as a member, but whose name he cannot recall. The fire at the time he saw it had apparently just started and had not reached serious proportions. He immediately got a Are extinguisher from the Senate side, thereby passing the flame and upon operating it found that it had no retarding effect, because it had gained great headway in that brief space of time. The sergeant and one or two other men had arrived then and got ready the hose that was stationed at the Speaker's door, but the blaze was already coming out from the reading room so that they were compelled to abandon it, and got the hose in operation from the west corridor, while other constables with the caretaker of the Senate reading room had also a line of hose operating from the Senate side, but even then found the smoke so dense that they were unable to get any results and were forced away from that part of the building, by which time the fire brigade had arrived, the police then bent their energies to warning those in rooms and in getting them out of the building, as it was evident that the conflagration was going to be serious.
I regret to say that in addition to the two ladies who died by suffocation in Mr. Speaker's quarters five others are reported missing, and I fear have perished,-
Mr. Haw, member of Parliament for Yarmouth, N.S.
Mr. J. B. R. Laplante, assistant clerk, House of Commons.
Mr. Robert Fanning, Post Office Department.
Mr. Alphonse Desjardins, plumber, Publio Works Department.
Constable Alphonse Desjardins, Dominion Police Force.
I have no reason to believe the fire was the result of a malicious act, but would suggest that a board of inquiry be constituted to fully investigate all the facts, and if possible to ascertain the true cause.
(Sgd.) A. P. Sherwood,
Chief Commissioner of Police.

speechtext:
On motion of Sir Thomas White (Minister of Finance) the House went into committee, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair, to consider the following proposed resolution:
That it is expedient to amend the Bank Act by repealing the provision limiting the time within which chartered banks may lend money for the purchase of seed grain upon the security of the grain purchased, the crops to be grown therefrom and the seed thrashed from the crop ; and also by- permitting the chartered banks to lend money to farmers and those engaged in raising stock upon the security of their live stock, that is to say, upon horses and their progeny, bulls and cows and their progeny, sheep and swine.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The resolution
is sufficiently plain as to the nature of the legislation which we propose to introduce, but if, at this stage, any further explanation is desired, I shall be glad to give it.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I wish my
hon. friend would give the information now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The House will recall that last year we amended the Bank Act by providing that banks might make loans upon the security of " grain purchased, the drops to be grown therefrom, and the seed threshed from the crop." By the terms of that legislation the time was limited practically to last year. It was stated in the House that it was desirable that production should be encouraged' in every way and it was thought we might for that year, on account of its being war time, enact this legislation. The legislation has given some .satisfaction. I have no doubt that good results have followed its enactment, and it is now proposed to take away the time limit which was imposed by the legislation of last year so that this year the banks may continue to make advances to farmers to enable them to purchase seed grain, and take the security which the legislation of last year enabled them to take.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Do you propose to make it permanent?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
The legislation
is permanent as drafted, but if, while the Bill is before the House or the committee, it is thought desirable that a further limit should be placed upon it, I shall raise no objection.
The other provision of this Bill involves a considerable departure. At successive revisions of the Bank Act the question has been raised as to whether a bank shall be permitted to take security upon live stock, under what is now section 88 of the Act. There has been a considerable divergence of view on this point, in the past. In drafting the Bill previous to the last revision of the Bank Act, I provided that a bank should be authorized to loan to ranchers on the security of their cattle, and if my memory serves me, also upon the security of their horses. When the matter was under consideration by the Banking and Commerce Committee, and by the House of Commons, it was thought advisable not to enact that provision and it was accordingly withdrawn. The difficulty that has arisen on every occasion when this matter has been under discussion in the House, respecting this provision, which has been asked for by many, enabling the banks to loan upon the security of the live stock of the farmer, has been the question of notice to creditors. The House is aware that, under section 88, the bank is permitted to take security upon raw material and manufactures in their various stages of produc-431
tion without registration. The matter has been fully discussed in the House and I think it is not necessary for me to advert further to that aspect of it. I pointed out last year, when the matter was under consideration, that there were thousands of transactions taking place daily throughout Canada whereby liens were given to banks upon raw material, or upon manufactures in process of completion, or upon goods, under section 88 of the Bank Act. No notice is required to be given to the public by registration or otherwise as to these liens. As far as giving liens upon live stock is concerned, it has been felt every time that this matter has been before the House in the past, that it was advisable, not only in the interests of the public and of creditors, but also in the interest of the farmers themselves, that such notice should be given. But, there were difficulties in the way of giving notice by registration or otherwise. Most of the provinces of Canada have what is known as chattel mortgage, or bill of sale, legislation under which mortgages and bills of sale upon personal property which remains in the visible possession of its owners shall not be valid as against creditors, unless registered in accordance with the laws of the provinces. Most of the provinces of Canada have legislation of that character. On the other hand, there is at least one province, Quebec, in which chattel mortgages or bills of sale are not recognized, and where there is consequently no provision for their registration. The legislation that I now propose has in the past failed to become law because of the difficulties of giving notice by registration. The Dominion itself has no organized machinery for the purpose of receiving and filing chattel mortgages, liens on live stock, or bills of sale, which might be taken by banks as security. The only organization at hand is the provincial organization, and in order to draft a Bill that would meet the requirements of the situation it would be necessary to name officials in the several provinces and under the jurisdiction of the several provincial governments, who would receive, file, and keep records of these liens, chattel mortgages or bills of sale. Therefore, this legislation has not so far been enacted.	.
Strong representations have been made to me that this legislation is very desirable. It has been pointed out, particularly from the West, that the enactment of this legislation would facilitate the making of further advances, affording a greater degree of credit to those engaged in the live stock

industry; and also that the banks would be more willing to loan substantial sums, and for longer periods, if they were permitted to take the securities referred to in this Act. It is further pointed out with, regard to cattle, that it is very desirable that they should be reared to maturity in Canada rather than sold when young and finished on the other side of the line. For all these and other considerations which I need not mention too minutely, there appears to be a very considerable public demand for this legislation.

Has the demand for this legislation come from the banks or from the farmers?	.
Sir THOMAS WHITE. It comes from the farmers. I received only recently a resolution from the United Farmers of Alberta in favour of this legislation, and it has been brought to my attention that the farmers of Manitoba were also in favour of it. Hon gentlemen will be able to tell me whether that is also the case in Saskatchewan. Tbs demand has not come from tile banks, as I shall show my !hon. friend in a few moments. I have been aware that this demand existed, and that it was the view of those engaged in stock rearing that this would afford very considerable assistance to the communities engaged in that industry. Consequently, some time ago I took the subject up and gave it my best attention and consideration. It was brought to my attention that in the United States a very large business is done by banks loaning upon chattel mortgage security covering live stock, and that the facilities afforded under the system which they have in vogue in the western states has greatly promoted that industry. I communicated with the several banks of Canada and asked their views as to whether the enactment of legislation of this character would result in increased 'accommodation being afforded the farmers and those engaged in the live stock industry. I asked them further, whether in their opinion there would he ample credits afforded during rthe coming year for the needs of the agricultural community and those engaged in the live stock industry. I received answers from all the banks, and I think they were about equally divided in opinion. About one-half were of the opinion that while not objecting to this legislation they would lend as freely if the legislation were not enacted as if it were enacted, and that they would necessarily continue to look to the personal

credit and standing of the borrower. Some of them added that they were not particularly favourable to the legislation but thought it might be of some assistance. On the other hand, a number of the banks held the view very strdngly that this legislation would result in the extension of substantial further credits to the farming community and would be of great advantage to the live stock industry. They said that with legislation of this Character they would feel justified in making more substantial advances and for longer terms. My answer to the hon. gentleman, in a word, is, that the demand for this legislation has come from the farming community, and particularly those engaged in the live stock industry, and that as to the banks, while there is a division of opinion among them as to the benefits likely to result from this legislation in the way of extension of credit, they are generally of the opinion that it will be of benefit.
I had to consider then the question which in the past has been the obstacle to the enactment of this legislation, namely the question of the rights of creditors, and of giving notice of these liens. I gave the matter ^he best consideration of which I was capable and, after canvassing the several ways which occurred to me, the Bill has been drafted so as to enable banks to take chattel mortgages or bill of sale upon live stock according to the laws of the several provinces. That is to say, a bank is put in precisely the same position as an individual or an institution that has the power to loan upon chattel mortgage or bill of sale security. I thought that was a wise conclusion, for this reason: the provinces have deemed it expedient, and in the public interest, to enact legislation protecting the rights of creditors. Unless there is some strong objection, it has seemed to me we ought to respect, so far as we can, the legislation in that regard of the several provinces. We have respected that legislation. In the Bill which I shall introduce, in the case of the provinces in which no provision for registration exists, we provide a simple method whereby notice may be given in the official gazette. I have, in a general way, covered the ground, but I desire to say further that {he Bill will be referred to the Banking and Commerce Committee. ' I need not say how much confidence I have in that committee. There are some first-class lawyers amongst its members, and if any better method can be suggested for giving notice * of this legisla-

tion, I shall be only too glad to give it my best consideration, and if possible, to adopt it-

When this matter was before the House on a previous occasion, I took very strong ground against legislation of this kind being effected. I still think it would be very objectionable to pass such an Act, because it would enable the banks to strengthen their security, as they would naturally do. While they might lend money to the farmer, they would take very good care to have him sign the printed form which they would always have available, and by means of which he would pledge to the bank all his horses, swine and cattle. Whether the debt was a large one or a small one, the words used would be of a general character, and it seems to me that the result would be that the credit of the farmer with the storekeeper, from whom he must continually purchase his supplies, would be very much impaired, and in the end this would result to the disadvantage of the farmer rather than to his benefit. The minister, I see, has to a certain extent met that objection by providing that the notice of these securities shall be published in the Canada Gazette.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In the Gazette of the provinces. In the provinces in which chattel mortgages and bills of sale are recognized, and in which provision is made for their registration, a chattel mortgage or bill of sale must be registered in accordance with the provincial law. But in the province of Quebec, and in other provinces in which there is no provision under the provincial law for the registration of a chattel mortgage or bill of sale, within a certain number of days after the taking of the chattel mortgage or bill of sale by the bank notice must be given to the officials of the provincial Gazette.

Can the -minister give us any information as to the extent to which advantage has been taken by the banks in regard to the legislation which was pa-ss-ed last year giving them wider powers than -they had had previously in the w-ay of taking securities on grain. Is the -minister aware of the extent to which advantage was taken of the advances?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I have no definite information on the -matter, b-ut I understand that the -legislation was an advantage.

I live in a portion of Saskatchewan in which advances would probably be made by the banks to farmers for seed grain, if -such a practice was to be carried into effect, and the answer of the minister is in accord with the information I have. I am a practising solicitor, and I never heard of any instance in which a seed grain lien was taken by a bank. I would point out further to the -minister that under the legislation of last year, in the case of a lien which the bank -could take or of a lien which was not registered, the document could be put in the banker's desk. Notwithstanding that, we have provision in our provincial -statute providing for the -registration of mortgages taken in respect of -seed grain. Is it -intended that the provincial law shall govern the registration of documents taken fo-r advances on seed grain, cattle, and other things?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
We propose
, merely to take away the time limitation which was imposed last year. Under this legislation it will not be necessary for a seed grain lien to be registered.

If advances on live stock and cattle are to be put under the provincial law, why not advances for seed grain? I must say that I do not think the officials whose duty it is to register seed grain liens will -be troubled with many of them. You may lead a horse to water, but you cannot make him drink; the minister is leading the banks up to the trough, but
[Mr. Pugslev.1
I doubt very much whether, by this legislation, he will be able to induce them to give any further credit to the farmers.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Why will not the banks give any more credit to the farmers?

The reason is that the advances they make at the present time are on the personal credit of the farmer. I am satisfied, or at least I will take the minister's word for it, that the legislation will be useful in big operations in the ranching country, but, like my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), I fear for the small farmer. The tendency in our country is to limit the extent to which security can be given, and in that connection I would point to the amendment of the Saskatchewan Chattel Mortgage Act, which provides that ordinary exemptions will apply to chattel mortgages as well as to executions. There is a good deal of talk, particularly amongst bankers, about our farmers going in for mixed farming. We have had wise essays and long lectures as to our farmers changing their methods of agriculture. To the ordinary young banker out on the prairies, mixed farming expresses itself in hogs. The young banker out there frequently gets instructions from his head office to do all he can to induce his farmer customers to go into mixed farming, and his instructions usually specify that half of any advance he makes to a farmer shall be invested in mixed farming. As I have said, mixed farming to the young banker usually means hogs, -so that if he makes an advance of $200 to a farmer he insists that $100 shall be invested in hogs. A friend of mine in Saskatchewan, near the border of Alberta, told me some time ago that he saw ten or a dozen young dead pigs close to a barn. The banker had loaned $200 to the farmer, and had insisted that $100 be invested in 'hogs. The farmer bought the hogs, but he had no means of sustaining them, and they died of starvation. That is mixed farming according to the banker, and if we don't look out we are going to have trouble on account of bankers interfering with our methods of agriculture. I do not want to come to a final conclusion at the moment, but my own view is that the minister is not doing a good thing for the small farmer in this legislation. I think in some way he should distinguish between loans which are made to cattle men and loans which are made to farmers who have only a small amount

of stock. He might distinguish between the two classes by saying, for instance, that loans of $2,000 should come under this legislation, but nothing under that.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: In answer to my hon. friend, I would say that I have never been in any way censorious as to the class of farming that is done in any particular province. I always assume that those engaged in & business know the best way of carrying that business on. My hon. friend says quite truly that men write essays and give lectures as to what class of farming should be carried on, but after all the farmer kn-'-w3 best what kind of farming he should engage in. I have always .said that. So far as this legislation is concerned, the remarks of my hon. friend are most interesting to me. What my hon. friend from St. John has said, has been said upon many previous occasions when this legislation has been before the House. The one desire that I have in this legislation is to facilitate, as far as I can, the granting of credits to the rural communities in order to enable them to carry on their industry to better advantage. If the Banking and Commerce Committee is of the opinion that the small farmer should be exempt from this legislation, I shall be inclined to attach great weight to their view, because I know that this question will be very thoroughly discussed by the committee. We have only one object in introducing this legislation, and if1 any part of this Bill is likely to be 'controversial, I shall be only too willing to drop it. I may say, however, that the legislation has been brought forward for no other purpose than to meet the needs of a growing industry in the West, as presented to me by the parties engaged in that industry. If it is thought desirable by the Banking and Commerce Committee, or by the House, that this legislation should be limited to dealers in live stock only, I shall be glad to give their opinion my most earnest and best consideration. But I know that in the past there has been, and I believe there is to-day, a very substantial body of opinion, both in this House and outside, in favour of granting legislation such as this, which the farmer need not avail himself of, but which he may avail himself of in order to facilitate the rearing of live stock to maturity. I know that in certain sections of the West, and other parts of the rural community, this legislation is considered of very great import-

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
I think it is an undoubted fact that bankers as -a rule do not favour lending to farmers. Banks are rather created for the purpose of active trade, and I believe that some time ot other we shall have banks in Canada intended especially for farmers. This resolution deals with two classes of goods belonging to farmers: grain, and live stock.
I understand that the purpose of the resolution is to give banks the power to take a lien upon live stock, and to have the lien published or registered. I do not quite understand the reason for the first part of this proposition:	-
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Bank Act by repealing the provision limiting the time within which chartered banks may lend money for the purchase of seed grain upon the security of the grain purchased, the crops to be grown therefrom and the seed thrashed from the crop.
Under the cir cum stances, I am sorry to say, I am not able to get a copy of the Statutes, and consequently I do not know exactly what is meant. If I understand my hon. friend correctly, the law as it is to-day provides that banks can advance money upon grain, and it is now proposed to withdraw that power from the banks.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No. I can quite understand why my hon. friend misunderstands the situation. Last year we gave this power to the banks for one year only. We are now proposing to take away that limitation of 'time, so that the banks may continue to lend to the farmers upon the security in question.

This idea originated in my section of the country. It really developed out oif the practice adopted by the Lethbridge Board of Trade, which, finding that the farmers in that district couM not get credit at the banks, formed what is known as the Lethbridge live stock guarantors, a body composed of some fifty of the business men of the city of Lethbridge. This body guarantees the payment to the bank of money advanced to farmers in the immediate district for the purchase of live stock. The scheme worked splendidly, and assisted materially in the development of mixed farming. The farmers thought that they should be able to get this credit direct from the bank. The matter came before the United Farmers Association, at its recent meeting in the city of Calgary, and they endorsed the idea contained in this resolution of the Minister of Finance.
ance.

In my section of the country "there are a great many people who have come from the United States. They dislike our banking system; in fact the banking system of Canada is extremely unpopular amongst the farmers of Western Canada, not because they want to get something from the banks for which they do not give an equivalent, but because they cannot get anything in many cases from the banks, and the American farmers argue in favour of the state or local bank which exists in the- United States. One argument in favour of that is the fact that they can secure small loans by giving small chattel mortgages. I agree with the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney), that a great many essays and lectures are delivered by the heads of the Canadian banks to the farmers as to how they should farm their land, and telling them they should go in for mixed farming and abandon mining the land. Those very bankers, however, are the men who refuse to permit the farmers to go into mixed farming. In 1914, during the drought which existed in Southern Alberta, the farmers had a great many hogs, but on account of the failure of the crop they had no feed on their own farms, and so they went to the banks and asked for an advance on the strength of this live-stock, so that they could get feed for them. What happened? The banks would not give them a cent, and the farmers were forced to sell their hogs at a price away below the market price because they had no feed for them, and because the banks would not provide an advance so that they could buy feed. In many cases the farmers were responsible men, but the banks seem to have had an attack of cold feet in Southern Alberta that summer; they were afraid of the country; they did not think it would amount to anything; but I think I am safe in saying that last- year Southern Alberta, which was drought-stricken the year before, had as good a crop as three average crops. In that area of country the average' crop has been greater than the average yield in any country during any one season. If the farmers are to go into mixed farming, they must have assistance from the banks. I do not want to attack the banks for their attitude during the past year, but their attitude has been the same during all years. They are not giving assistance in many cases to the farmers of Western Canada, and I presume the same is the case throughout the rest of the country. A bank sends out a young fMr. Buchanan.]
man to manage a branch in a small community surrounded by farmers, and he can hardly advance a cent to farmers without receiving sanction from the head office. He has to communicate with Toronto or Montreal, and a farmer having an opportunity of investing a small amount in a horse or a cow may have passed away before the manager receives the sanction of the head office. There will have to be some change in the method of management of the banks before the western farmer is satisfied.

I
suppose this is hardly the time to discuss this question generally, but I want to ask the minister one question. Before I do so,
I would like to refer to some points which have come up. It is rather early to say very much oil, this question, but at present I do not see much cause to be quite as afraid of the effect of this legislation as my hon. friends from St. John (Mr. Pugsley) and Saskatoon (Mr. McCraney) apparently are, although when we discuss the question further, we may change our minds.
With regard to the -increased loans, I have not heard of any in my own own locality, but we have better authority than my experience, and I am always prepared to submit to better authority when I find it. The Grain Growers' Guide of Winnipeg has taken the trouble to make inquiries among the farmers throughout the country, and I find in a recent issue of that journal-it was unfortunately destroyed, and I therefore cannot quote from it-that a number of the answers received showed that the recent * legislation had caused a very considerable increase in the loans to farmers, and that it also had made it possible for farmers, who otherwise would not have received loans, to get them. Now, I am inclined to think that some good has been done.
With regard to the difficulty raised by my hon. friend from Saskatoon as to a banker insisting on a farmer buying hogs or something of -that kind with a portion of the money advanced, I do not see that the situation will be any worse than it is, at present, if the legislation proposed by the minister is passed. There is nothing to prevent a banker from insisting on that sort of thing if he is giving a loan of any kind. The question I want to ask is thil:	My hon.
friend from Saskatoon referred to recent legislation in Saskatchewan regarding chattel mortgages providing that a chattel mortgage shall not affect property which is exempt from seizure under execution.

My hon. friend (Sir Thomas White) proposes to recognize the existing legislation of the provinces at least so far as registration is concerned. Is he proposing to recognize that existing legislation now? Supposing a bank takes a mortgage on a farmer's exemptions, will they be affected? Without expressing a definite opinion on the question just now, I think there is a good deal to be said in favour of recognizing recent legislation in Saskatchewan or in any other province-that shall pass such legislation. I am not asking my hon. friend to decide positively whether the legislation is going to be recognized now, but I would like to hear his opinion, because the subject is worthy of his consideration. The difficulty has been raised about loans to small farmers who have a very small amount of stock but if mortgages -on exemptions are ineffective that difficulty will be largely removed.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I have followed
the principle of recognizing provincial legislation with respect to bills of sale and chattel mortgages, and in the Bill which I intend to introduce founded on this resolution, it is provided that:	,
13.	The security agreement may be fnade in the form of a bill of sale or chattel mortgage, or, in any province where no provision exists in the laws of the province for the filing or other registration of bills of sale or chattel mortgages, then in the form H in the schedule to this Act or in a form to like effect.
14.	Such security agreement shall be filed or otherwise registered in accordance with, and shall be subject to the laws relating to hills of sale or chattel mortgages, as the case may he, that are in force in the province in which the live stock included in such security agreement are situate.
I am not sure that that touches the point the hon. gentleman has in view. He has in mind the fact that in Alberta there are certain exceptions which cannot be made the subject of a chattel mortgage. I think that this clause will cover them/ but, if not, I shall be glad if he will give me the benefit of his information after the Bill is introduced, and I will have the matter discussed in the Banking and Commerce Committee.

I have a word
to say on behalf of the mixed-farming country and of the small farmer- When the Bank Act was up for consideration some years ago, this matter was threshed out very thoroughly. On that occasion, certain members of the House, both on our side and on the Government side, took a strong position as to the propriety of including such a provision as is made here.
I am sorry that at that time the minister did not agree with us, and am correspondingly glad to see that he has come around to what seems to me to be a very much better view. I hope that when the Bill gets into the Banking and Commerce Committee he will not be swerved from his present intention of including all classes of stock farming, whether on a large scale or on a small scale. I do not anticipate the difficulties that have been suggested by some hon. members. The purpose of this legislation, as I understand it, is to enable the banks, as the reser.voir of the money of the people, to loan part of the funds in a manner they are not now permitted to do by the Bank Act. I cannot understand that this enabling provision as regards the use by the banks of money in their care is likely to result, or'can result, in aDy detriment to those who may be looking for the advantage of the use of ithat money.
Resolution reported and concurred in.
Sir THOMAS WHITE thereupon moved for leave to-introduce Bill No. 33, to amend the Bank Act. ,

stagedirection
speechtext:
Oil the Orders of the Day:
Hon. J. D- HAZEN (Minister pf Marine and Fisheries):	Mr. Speaker, as a matter
of privilege, I desire to refer to a subject that, I think, is of sufficient importance to justify me in asking the indulgence of the House for a few minutes. My attention has been called to an article appearing in the Ottawa Evening Journal of February 9, headed: " Germans Have Access to Confidential Papers in Ottawa," and reprinting an article contained in the Toronto Star of the same date which, among other things, Says this:.
Probably the most conspicuous case on record Is that of Gustav Heidmann, secretary of the Minister of Marine, and Naval Service, Hon. J. D. Hazen. Mr. Heidmann was horn in Germany, and no doubt has relatives fighting there. He has been a long time in Canada, and is reputed as an able and efficient secretary. His name appears on the most recent list issued from the Secretary of State's Department as having received full naturalization. But Mr. Heidmann has access to all correspondence connected with Canadian coast defence, wireless, harbour patrols, and marine matters which come to the office of the Minister of' Marine and naval defence. It is not conceivable that Admiral Von Tirpitz would he so trustful, in connection with the administration of his department.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
I think it desirable that I should state the facts to the House. My secretary, Mr, Heidmami, who has been my secretary since November, 1911, was bom in Germany, and, when an infant in arms only a few weeks old, came to Canada with his parents who were dissatisfied with conditions in Germany and sought Canada with a view to making their home here and becoming citizens of this country. The father settled in Toronto, and, soon after taking up his residence there, applied to an alderman of that city for naturalization as a British subject, and received a certificate which he believed conferred upon him the rights of a British subject, but about which there may be some question as the preliminary steps were not entirely complied with. However, for over thirty-two years Mr. Heidmanm's father has engaged in manufacturing business in Toronto, has voted at elections from time to time, and has taken such part in the affairs of the city as a good citizen ought to take. Mr. Heidmann, my secretary, was brought up in Toronto, educated in the common schools there, and, after having received his education, was appointed as private secretary to Mr. H. S. Strathy, General Manager of the Traders Bank of Canada, which bank, I believe, has since been amalgamated with the Royal Bank of Canada. In 1904 Mr. Heidmann came to Ottawa as a member of the Civil Service of Canada, and he continued in the Service until 1911, being at that time assistant to the secretary of the National Transcontinental Railway Commission. In 1911, I selected Mr. Heidmann, as my secretary out of a number of applicants, because I thought him eminently fit for the position. Before making that selection, I made inquiries regarding Mr. Beidmann's character and standing, from persons in . the city of Toronto, who knew him and his family well; in whom I had every confidence, -and in whom the members of this House would have every confidence if I were to mention their names, as they are among the leading citizens of that city. The reports I received from them were of the most favourable character, with regard to Mr. Heidmann's character and abilities, and also with regard to the standing and reputation of his family who had been living in Toronto, as I have said, for thirty-two years. Since then Mr. Heidmann has acted as my secretary and has done so with 'great acceptability t(o myself, 'because of the industry .and ability 
with which he has discharged his duties. I may say for the information of the House that one of his brothers, soon after the outbreak of the war, enlisted and is now a trooper in the third troop, " C " squadron, Second Brigade, Fourth Canadian Mounted Rifles, which has since been reorganized into an infantry brigade finder the command of General Victor Williams and has been in the .trenches in Flanders for some considerable time fighting for the defence of Canada and the Empire, and for the perpetuation of those democratic principles that are so dear to the heart of every Canadian. In a letter which was received only a short time ago from Colonel F. B. Black, a member of the legislature of the province of New Brunswick, and who is also serving his country at the front, he spoke in the highest possible terms of the services which were being rendered by Mr. Heidmann's brother in the trenches and referred to the fact that he had been offered promotion on several occasions but had declined it because he preferred to remain, as he stated, with his " pals " in the ranks, and to continue side by side with those with whom he had been serving since the outbreak of the waj;.
My secretary, until a short time ago, believed that he was a British subject. Believing that his father had been naturalized, and he himself having lived in Toronto since he was an infant, he considered that he was a British subject. But there being some legal question about it, he applied for, and obtained full naturalization at the time of the outbreak of the war. I think it is only right and fair that I should make this statement to the House in view of the article I have read from the Toronto Star, and which was copied last evening into the Ottawa Evening Journal. I would like to say further, that after the war broke out, when rumours became current in Ottawa in regard to Mr. Heidmann, and on different occasions since, he has come to me and told me that if, in the slightest degree, I felt embarrassed in consequence of his connection with me as private secretary, he would at once, and without any feeling, tender his resignation and seek to make a living in some other way.
Mr. Heidmann is married to an Ottawa lady connected with some of the most prominent and oldest families in the capital. He is the father of five children who are being brought up as good Canadians and good British subjects. I declined to allow

him to resign because I felt that if I did so, or if I accepted his resignation, or gave him some position in the service that was not as important as the position he held, I would he doing a very great injustice to a young man who, I believe, is in every way an upright, conscientious, and competent public official, and who, I further believe, is as loyal a Canadian and as loyal a Britisher as can be found within the four corners of the Dominion of Canada.
This matter, previously to its being taken up by the press, was the subject of comment, and 1 had hoped that the result of the investigation which was carried on then by the Ottawa Free Press would have put an end to the rumours that were then in circulation. I might quote this from the Ottawa Free Press published in November, 1914:
Another Rumour Run to Earth.
For several days past the Free Press has been in .receipt of communications calling attention to the fact that a gentleman holding a confidential position in one of the Government Departments in Ottawa is a native of Germany. Upon this fact has been built a formidable structure of suspicion. The Free Press has just completed a very thorough inquiry. It started out with a strong doubt as to the propriety of the retention of such a one in a capacity giving him access to important and possibly secret governmental information. These doubts have been dispelled. The loyalty and sincerity of the young man have been vouched for, not only by his minister and his deputy minister, but by a large number of responsible Ottawa people. An interview with him has given the Fress Press the same impression; and further, even in the position he holds, he has access to no information that would be of value to the enemy.
That last statement is absolutely correct. Any secret information in connection with the department over which I have the honour to preside is known only to the deputy minister . and myself and, on some rare occasions, to the Chief of Staff and the Director of the Naval Service. The article in the Free Press concluded:
Don't let us get into a silly war panic. Don't let us permit anybody's reputation to be blasted by irrational rumours. The warning seems necessary because this is not the first time since the war began that the Free Press has felt called upon to defend an Ottawa citizen from cruel injustice.
I feel that a very cruel injustice is being done to my secretary by the publication of such articles as appeared last night in the Ottawa Journal, and an injustice which must bring sorrow and tribulation not only to himself, but to his wife and the members of his family. Therefore, I deem it my duty as his chief, and as one whom he has served
with the very greatest possible loyalty and fidelity during the time I have been Minister of Marine and Fisheries, to say these few words to the House, not only as a matter of justice to my private secretary, but in order that there may be to some extent removed from the public mind the unfortunate conclusions that have been drawn from evidence and facts that are entirely insufficient to justify even the slightest suspicion being attached to Mr. Heid-mann's loyalty and fidelity.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: On the Orders of the Day: '

subtopic: GERMAN CANADIANS IN THE MILITARY SERVICE.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to draw to the attention of the hon. Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) an interview which appears in the Ottawa Journal of the 9th of this month. I do this not for the purpose of making comment on it or finding any fault, at present at all events; but I think it very much better - that in cases like that to which I am going to call attention, as well as the case to which the Minister of Marine has called attention, the matter should be

brought up in Parliament and a fair and frank statement made. The Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Hazen) should - not be too censorious on either the newspapers or the people throughout the country who have written and spoken with reference to the subject of his complaint. I know there has been a good deal of talk, and I think it much better that the minister should bring the matter before Parliament and make a statement as he has done, because it tends to remove erroneous impressions, and to allay suspicion and anxiety. The press and people of this country are naturally exceedingly anxious and sensitive at the present time. I have called the minister's attention to this interview in the Journal and he has given me permission to bring the matter up. The interview is as follows:
" There is an erroneous impression in the country," saifi General Hughes to-day, " that there is some German officer around Ottawa doing intelligence work. That German officer is at the front in the trenches. He is one of hundreds of Germans loyally fighting with Canada under the British flag." The Minister of Militia was referring to newspaper comment on statements made some time ago by the Minister of Militia that Capt. Kahn, his chief intelligence officer, was a German with two brothers fighting in the German army, that he was the son of a German officer and that his mother was the daughter of an Austrian General.
" It is remarkably strange," continued General Hughes, " that they do not state that thirtj'-eight Germans have fallen in the service fighting the battles of the Empire with the Canadian forces. It would be better if those who are endeavouring to make a race war out of it would follow their example. This is not a race war, but a war of liberty.
" There is an agitation all over the country regarding military protection for civic works, such as water works. This is a pyrely municipal matter in which the Militia Department has no concern. If the people would throw fewer cigarette or cigar butts around there would be fewer fires. Twice in three weeks there have been fires in the reading room of Parliament.
" In the South African war," he said, " I had the honour of enlisting the first Boer in the British service. There never were truer men or better fighters once they realized the difference between Boer and British liberty."
Would the Minister of Militia kindly state whether that interview is correct, and if - it is not, in what particulars it is incorrect?

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
subtopic: GERMAN CANADIANS IN THE MILITARY SERVICE.
speechtext:
I did not state that Captain Hahn-not Kahn, as in the newspaper-had any relatives fighting against the British in the Austrian or German forces. His father is a very estimable resident of the city of Stratford. In his younger days he was in the German army, 
but, like many another splendid resident of Canada and the United States to-day, he left Germany on account of the tyrannous government in that country, and the spread of militarism. He came to Canada as a citizen and has been a most estimable citizen ever since. His son, I am proud to say, is following in the footsteps of his father, and is now fighting splendidly at the front for the cause of liberty. He has already, rton the Distinguished Service Order a!t the front in the British service.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
In my absence yesterday a question was raised regarding the purchase of horses, into the details of which I shall not enter. Some observations were made concerning horses purchased in the Kings county region in Nova Scotia in comparison with those purchased in Prince Edward Island and other parts. The horses purchased by Major Anderson in New Brunswick for his battery cost upwards of $225 each. The horses purchased in Prince Edward Island cost, I think, an average of $175.50. The horses purchased in Sydney, C.B., I understand, cost $185 and upwards. These, taken all in all, were good horses. The horses purchased in the Kings county region cost on an average $171.09. Soon after the camp started, when these horses commenced coming in, I remember one morning, when I was out bright and early, seeing a number of horses coming into camp. I admired most of them as they passed, for they were in splendid condition. I asked whence they came, and was assured that they came from the vicinity of Kings county, in Nova Scotia. They were without exception the finest looking lot I had seen come into camp. Towards the tail of the procession there were about twenty-two horses that were rather dried up looking, and four horses that certainly never should have been allowed inside the camp; I am free to admit that, but it is an old game, I understand, among some of these smart-alec horse dealers to change horses in the cars when they are loading and things like that. Any one who set eyes on these four would have realized that they were swapped horses, and that the other twenty-two were not up to the standard. I immediately held them up, and made inquiries, and I was informed that they had been for forty-eight
hours without food or water in a car standing in a yard somewhere along the line. Four of them were disposed of as no good, but the other twenty-two-I am not exactly sure whether the number was twenty-two or twenty-one-were placed in suitable quarters and given lots of food and water, and at the end of two weeks they were a lot of very fine looking animals. I say this without prejudice to anybody. I do not wish to raise any controversial issue to-day, but I am prepared to enter into the details of this transaction on any occasion if any one chooses to bring it up. I do not want to make it a political issue, but if any one cares to make it such I am prepared to discuss it as a political issue. If any one wants to treat it as a business issue, I am prepared to treat it as a business issue. 'So fax as the horses purchased in Kings county are concerned, I say that they were about the cheapest horses purchased in the Maritime Provinces. They were better than the horses purchased in the Westmorland region, and better by 30 or 35 per cent than the horses purchased at Sydney.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition

Royal Northwest Mounted Police-Northwest territories, Yukon territory, provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan-pay of force, $630,216.75.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I might make
some explanation of this vote. The members will observe that there is a reduction of $280,356. That is due to the fact that the force has been reduced. On the outbreak of war the force was increased to 1,200 noncommissioned officers and constables, and a number of men were engaged specially for one year's service . Of these about 300 took their discharge in August and September last, the large majority joining overseas forces, and owing to the peaceable demeanour of persons of enemy nationality and the presence of large bodies of troops in training in the provinces of Alberta and Saskatchewan, it was not considered neces-

sary to keep the force up to its strength of, 1,200-900 non-commissioned officers ' and constables being considered sufficient. When the commissioner's recommendation of this decrease, concurred in by the comptroller, was brought to my attention, I gent a copy of the report to my right hon. friend the leader of the Opposition before taking any action on it. I thought the matter was a proper one upon which to consult him, especially as for more than fifteen years he had been the political head of the force. He agreed with me that it would be safe to act upon the report of the commissioner and the comptroller, and the force was consequently reduced from 1,200 to 950, and the contemplated reduction is to 900. The present strength of the force is 950 officers and men, and 987 horses, distributed as follows :
Officers and
	men.	Horses.
Alberta	393	406Saskatchewan	445	559Northwest Territories...	22	2Yukon Territory . . . .	60	20Hudson Bay	30	950	987There are 10 divisional	posts	and 253 detachments.
With regard to the present arrangements between the Eederal Government and the provinces, information has already been given to the House in the Orders, in Council which I had the honour of laying on the table this afternoon. Briefly speaking, those arangements are as follows: the existing agreements will expire on the 31st of March, and arangements for their renewal have been entered into, the only difference being that they can be cancelled by either the Dominion or the Provincial Government on one year's notice being given. Each province pays $75,000 annually for the services of the force, and also pays for the maintenance of all prisoners and lunatics confined in Mounted Police guard rooms, and their transport expenses.
In connection with the work of the force for the past year, the attention of hon. members might be directed to the report of the comptroller of the force, which has already been laid on the table of the House. I think a portion of the report is of sufficient importance to read to the House, as it relates to a very important subject. I am reading from page 8:
When the war broke out, some natural apprehension was felt for the peace and good order of the Western provinces, owing to a

large percentage -of the population being of enemy nationality, and it was therefore decided that the strength of the Mounted Police should be increased. No disturbance of the public peace has taken place and the provinces of Saskatchewan and Alberta during the past twelve months have been singularly quiet and orderly This fortunate condition is due to a variety of causes, wise precautions, fair and impartial treatment by the authorities, and an admirable attitude of self-restraint on the part of the loyal population towards the enemy aliens, and the recognition by these nationalities that as long as they pursued their ordinary avocations, and refrained from inimical acts, they would not he molested nor interfered with.
Distributing reports have been received, and alarming rumours have been current, from time to time, all of which, no matter how trivial or improbable,' have been investigated and found to be baseless. However, there have been instances of individuals whose acts and words were treasonable and seditious. In a few cases, they were prosecuted and convicted.
The enemy nationalities are principally engaged in tilling the soil. They own their farms, have large interests, and have no intention of imperilling their property and their own security and safety.
I might say, in passing, that there was an intense desire all through the force to be permitted to enlist en masse. They would gladly have done so, but there were of course considerations which prevented that. The force had to be maintained at a suitable strength in the West in view of occurrences which might arise. The report continues:
The decrease in the strength is due to the fact that shortly after the outbreak of the war, authority was granted to increase the force by five hundred men for one year, and that nearly all the men so engaged took their discharges for the purpose of joining the army for service at the front. Many of them had joined because they thought that a contingent would be selected for active service. As this was not the case, they took the earliest opportunity of accomplishing their highly laudable and patriotic purpose.
The Comptroller, with whom I have discussed this subject, has made the significant statement that the influence of the women among the alien enemy portion of our population has been very beneficent. They are attached to the homes which they have established in the West, and appreciate, perhaps even more than the men, the liberties and privileges which they enjoy under the system of Government that is established and maintained in this country, and so their influence has been an important factor in bringing about the results to which I have alluded. The report continues:
They are scattered over the vast areas of these provinces, and it is quite apparent that
no concerted action could take place without preparation and organization, lacking which, any outbreak would be sporadic and fruitless.
The conditions for suppressing any such out- / break have greatly improved. Large bodies of troops are now under training at every centre.
For" the foregoing reasons, I recently reported to you that I did not consider it was necessary to maintain the strength at more than 900 and which recommendation you approved.
I have already spoken of the profound desire upon the part of the officers and men of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police to enlist for active service, but for the reasons I have indicated it was held impossible to grant their request. On the 25th day of August, 1914, this general order was made:
No leave of absence can be granted to officers, non-commissioned officers or constables of the force for the purpose of serving in any expeditionary force leaving Canada for the European war.
On the 3rd day of February, 1915, another general order was passed in the following terms:
Any non-commissioned officer or constable, who has less than three months to serve to complete his present engagement, may be permitted to purchase his discharge for the purpose of joining any contingent being raised for war services, provided he produces certificate that he will be enrolled in a contingent as above stated, if he is permitted to purchase his discharge, from the police.
This privilege is not to be extended to men who engaged for one year's service on account of the war.
I should also stale that these orders did not apply to Imperial reservists, about sixty in number, serving in the force, who were granted their discharge at the outbreak of the war to enable them to re-join the colours. The reason for that was that these men came to this country under a certain obligation as Imperial reservists. They joined the force under that obligation, and we thought it proper that they should not be prevented from filling an obligation that was binding on them at that time.
I am very glad, indeed, to be able to present to-the House the report with regard to the demeanour and behaviour of persons of enemy nationality in the western provinces. The spirit that has animated them throughout the war under somewhat trying conditions has been admirable, and the country is to be congratulated upon the comprehension and understanding of conditions as they exist, not only by persons of enemy nationality who have come to Canada for the purpose of making their home here, but by those of British or Canadian birth,
688	COMMONS
who are in large numbers in the western provinces, and who have shown a reason, able consideration for those settlers in the western part of our country who are of enemy nationality. Hon. gentlemen will remember that very early in the w*ar, on the 8th day of August, 1914, an Order in Council was passed; which, after reciting:
That there are many immigrants of German nationality quietly pursuing their usual avocations in various parts of Canada; that it is desirable that such persons should continue in such avocations without interruptionwent on to declare:
That such persons, so long as they quietly pursue their ordinary avocations, shall not toe arrested, detained, or interfered with unless there is reasonable ground to believe that they are engaged in .espionage, or attempting to engage in actions of a hostile nature, or to give information to the enemy, or unless they otherwise controvert any law, order in council, or proclamation.
That Order in Council, in the spirit in which it was promulgated, has commended itself to all elements of our population in Western Canada, with the results which, as they are embodied in the report of the Comptroller of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police, I have been very happy to announce to the House this afternoon. I desire also to pay a tribute to the Comptroller, Mr, Fortescue, and to the Commissioner, Mr. Perry, for the good judgment and discretion with which they have dealt with the few matters in regard to which it has been necessary for the police to take action on the lines indicated in the report.

That will be the case so long as it is commanded by such able officers as have been at its head for 'Some years past. Commissioner Perry is the one man who is exceptionally well qualified for the position he holds, and Mr. Fortescue has also had very long experience. I have been informed that Mr. Fortescue intends to take his pension at no distant date. Is my information correct?

Mr. Fortescue is advanced in years and his health is perhaps not as good as it was at. one time, so that I am not surprised to hear that 
he is contemplating taking his leave from the force. Every one will be sorry for this and I, who knew him well, will also be sorry to hear it. He is a most efficient man, most faithful in his duties, and my right hon. friend will be very lucky if he is able to secure as good a man to replace him. The work of the force at the present time in the older provinces of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta is decreasing. In those provinces it has no other duties than those of preventing and looking after offences against the common law which are found in every society- The offences prevalent at one time, such as tampering with cattle, are becoming fewer and fewer. I suppose for some years, oir perhaps for many years, we shall have to keep a cordon along the boundary line between Canada and the United States. I suppose also that my right hon. friend is increasing his patrol and his stations in the northern part of the country. As the force becomes less and less required in the older settlements that are included in the three provinces, settlement is spreading in the North, and I would like to know if my right hon. friend can tell me how many stations of the force he has outside of the boundaries of the provinces; in the Atha-baska-district, on the Peace river, on the Mackenzie river, and on Hudson bay.

men in all?

This will be

Sir ROBERT BORDEN; The policy is to withdraw the police from the towns, as far as possible, in order to utilize th-eir services in the rural districts. I am glad to hear the Prime Minister state that the conditions with regard to men of foreign birth are satisfactory, so far as the West is concerned, and that loyal citizens of Canada can feel that there is no disloyalty among the men who have come there to live. He spoke of the Order in Council of August 1914, as being, in effect, a message from the Canadian people as a whole to that section of our population and attributed to the provisions of that Order in Council some portion of the good results of which he spoke. But there is a growing feeling that the provisions of that Order in Council ought to be amended in relation to persons of foreign birth residing in Eastern Canada. Every hon. member must feel, having regard to information which, I ram sure, each of us is receiving from his people, that there has grown up in the mind of the average Canadian of to-day a great feeling of uncertainty and suspicion concerning people of German birth in their midst. In the West, you have communities made up of what may be called the plain people of central European countries, who have fled to Canada from the militaristic conditions under which they were living. But that does not describe the condition of affairs in the East. The people of Canada believe that there are in different localities a large number of people who are disloyal and who are in touch with the enemy. They note what * has taken place in the United States, where munition factories have been burned down and plots against life and property have been made, as is shown beyond the shadow of a doubt by the publication of the correspondence of attaches of both the Austrian and German
embassies in New York and Washington. There can be no doubt that these men have been in correspondence with spies throughout Canada. It is easy for us to publish to the world in a wholesale way concerning persons of German or Austrian birth residing in Canada that nothing will be said to him so long as he does not openly declare hostilities. But that is not sufficient, in my judgment. The time has come when something more must be done. If you have spies in the country, you may be sure that they are not shouting from the housetops the nature of their business. It is no answer to say that these men have gone to the front. The boys at the front write that the German troops seem to know all about what is going on among the Canadian sections there. A spy would probably be quite willing to go to the front in order to be able to gain information for the benefit of his country. At any rate, there can be no doubt that there is a feeling among the people of Eastern Canada that there are people among them who are in touch with the enemy. That is shown by letters which I received from Nova Scotia, and I am sure that my experience is not different from that of any other hon. members. The provisions of the Order in Council of August, 1914, ought to be made wider, and greater power should be given the Administration in order to deal with the cases-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would remind the hon. member that the item under consideration is the vote for the Royal North West Mounted Police, and I hope he will bring his remarks within the limits of the subject before the Chair.

You will remember, Sir, that the Prime Minister dealt with this very question. He spoke of the order of August, 1914, and dwelt upon the fact that its provisions, wide and generous as they were, had had good results amtong the foreign-born population in the West. Surely, I am in order in discussing the effect of that Order in Council, not only in regard to the West but in regard to the East as well. I do not want to go into the matter at too great length, but the same question was dealt with in another connection-if I am in order in referring to that-and I feel sure that the Prime Minister must attach importance to the representations in favour of a change in the provisions of that Order in Council. The utter disregard by the Germans and Austrians of the conditions that should ob-



tain between warring countries, is a sufficient reason why there should be, under the Defence of the Realm Act, the strongest kind of restraint upon all persons about whose loyalty there is any doubt. I have already said that I diaw a distinction between the case in the West and that of the East. The men who, coming from the common people of Central Europe, have fled from militarism and taken up pastoral pursuits in our West, are quite different from those who have come to the industrial centres of the East and who live under conditions that arouse the suspicions of the people among whom they dwell. There should be the widest possible scope given to the local authorities to deal with persons of that kind.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
So far as the principle set forth in the Order in Council is concerned, I think there cannot be much difference of opinion. The principle laid down is with respect to persons who have been invited to come to this country, and who have come here as settlers to make their home, to become Canadian citizens and to assist in cultivating, building up and developing this country. The Order in Council provides that such persons who quietly pursue their ordinary avocations, shall not be interfered with unless there is reasonable ground to believe that they are giving information to the enemy or performing other acts of an illegal or hostile nature, or otherwise contravene the law. I do not know what action we should take other than that with regard to persons who have come to this country practically on the invitation of the people of Canada, and who are engaged in the ordinary pursuit of their every day affairs, and are quiet, peaceable citizens. But the Government was not unmindful of the fact that there might be many persons of enemy nationality who might make some attempt at disorder, and so an Order in Council was passed on September 3, 1914, which was laid on the table last session, prohibiting the use or possession of fire-arms, ammunition, or dangerous explosives, in Canada by alien enemies. I need not Tead the Order in Council, which contained quite elaborate provisions. Then, on October 28, 1914, an Order in Council was passed providing for registration of alien enemies, for appointment of regktrars of alien enemies, prescribing regulations, providing for internment, and providing that no alien enemy, required to register, shall be naturalized unless he files 
the certificate of a registrar that he is registered and that -his application for naturalization is approved -by the registrar. This Order in Council also provides that no alien enemy shall be permitted to leave Canada without an exeat from a registrar to be issued only when the registrar is satisfied that such person will not assist the enemy. The Chief Commissioner of Dominion. Police may also, in any case, grant or cancel an exeat.
'Then, on November 20, 1914, provision was made for periodical reports to registrars by persons of enemy nationality, and so on. These provisions are all that seemed necessary, as far as the Government has been able to study the situation, and I think that the good effect of the orders which have been passed in that portion of Canada where the greatest number of alien enemies is to be found is the best possible proof that the regulations -are in accordance with sound judgment and good sense.

I am obliged to my right hon. friend the Prime Minister fox telling us about these official Orders in Council, but I think we might as well clear up the subject now. Matters are in an unsettled -state in Eastern Canada in regard to this question, because everybody recognizes the difference between the position of a farmer settled on the plains and a man who drifts into an industrial community in the East. Is there any provision in any Order in Council under which municipal or police authorities in any of our cities or towns can, upon ascertaining that a person is of alien or enemy birth or nationality, compel him to submit to surveillance, or to report at all times, or have they to depend upon the central authorities in Ottawa? I have in my mind the fact that in a community which adjoins my county there were two Germans living at the outbreak of the war. Shortly after the war broke out one of them went away. I reported to Ottawa at the request of the neighbours of the man who remained the fact that the other man was of alien birth, that he had only been in that place for a shirt time and that he was living on a farm. I suppose he was a man who eame within this Order in Council and who had been invited to come to Canada. I was told in reply that persons .would be sent down to investigate. They did investigate, and I was told afterwards that this man was perfectly harmless. However, it developed that he was not a perfectly harmless man, and

at the instance of the local authorities he was arrested and was, by various processes, eventually imprisoned at Halifax and then taken to the internment camp at Amherst. He escaped last summer from the internment camp by means which showed that he had at all times been an enemy and that he should have been interned. Doubt exists in a great many eastern communities in regard to matters of this kind. I had a letter to-day from my own constituency asking whether wider powers should not be given to the police authorities to deal with these men of foreign birth, at least in the four eastern provinces. These men who have come to this country and who, unfortunately, are Germans or Austrians, must pay the penalty. I wonder what our Canadian people would think if they were in Germany to-day. I think there should be the widest possible authority given to the police authorities to deal with persons of enemy nationality.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister what the aliens who have been interned in the Abitibi region, in the province of Quebec, are doing. Are they cultivating the land, or simply lumbering?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon. friend will have to wait for definite information on that point until the Estimates of the Department of Justice are reached, because the internment camps are all under the Minister of Justice.

I am not panicky, but
we must face the facts as they are. To emphasize what has been said by my hon. |riend from Piotou (Mr. Macdonald), I might give my personal experience. Last summer at Murray Bay, when the submarines which had been built by Vickers-Maxim at Montreal were undergoing their trials, there were for several days two spies in the district apparently surveying on the river Malbaie. The people at Murray Bay noticed them and immediately informed the police at Quebec. They did not get an answer as quickly as they expected, and, upon coming to me, I told them that they should wire to Col. Sherwood and he would direct the proper parties to have these persons looked after.
I do not know what became of the two spies; they disappeared as soon as they saw the brass buttons. But in the city of Quebec itself1-and my hon. friend from l'Islet (Mr. Paquette) can verify this statement-for one year before the war
there was a German named Mundschein-' they called him Moonshine down there- who had bought for a German syndicate, but apparently with the concurrence of some Canadian gentlemen, the extreme portion of the island of Orleans, just facing the Beaumont battery, which guards the city of Quebec and protects all that section of the river St. Lawrence. He had formed! a company which, I believe, came before this Parliament four sessions ago asking for a Bill authorizing them to erect some works there' It was found that Mundschein was a German spy who had been operating in Quebec. He was arrested and interned. This shows the audacity and the treachery of those people. My hon. friend, without being panicky, states what is the simple truth, that it is part of the highest German patriotism to act as a spy. Certainly these people will come into our cities with smiles and with graceful manners; but at the same time I say we should be on the look out at all times. What has been discovered in the United States as disclosed in the Von Papen papers and the revelations in San Francisco should open the eyes of the Canadian public. I am not panicky, but I say we must be very careful in guarding against the presence of these strangers in our midst.

I think it is only fair that while we are on this item of the Northwest Mounted Police, I should say a word in respect to that body, coming as I do from the city in which they have their headquarters and have had for many years. The mounted police in Western Canada, as I have known them, have been a body of men beyond reproach, perhaps the best body of men for the preservation of law and order that we have had in Western Canada or in tfie whole Dominion. I read not long ago the book of Colonel Steele, now General Steele, formerly an officer of the Northwest Mounted police, called "Forty Years in Western Canada. " That book gives one a very good idea of the pioneer work, of the hardships endured by that body of men in the earlier days of settlement all through the West. It was necessary in those days for the mounted poili-ce to go ahead of settlement and of civilization. They were the pioneers of civilization throughout the whole of Western Canada. A very interesting part of the book is the description of- the work of the police in British Columbia when the Canadian Pacific Railway was building its road into that province. They

also, of course, did work in connection with the construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway from the time that road first entered the Western country.
The mounted police, as a body of men, are to-day just as good a military organization as they were many years ago. We often hear in the West to-day and in the East from men who have been in the West, that the mounted police are not as good an organization as they were, say twenty-five years ago, in the matter of the preservation of law and order. My experience with the mounted police has been that they are today just as good a body of men as they were twenty-five years ago. All of us, especially men who are growing older, are inclined to look upon things that took place in the past as being greater than those which are taking place to-day.
That is as regard Governments.

As regards Governments it may be true. I also believe that we are inclined to look upon men living today as not 'being as great men as those who lived say twenty-five years ago. That may apply to statesmen as well as to ordinary individuals. However, in so far as the mounted police are concerned, I believe they are very well keeping up the traditions of the past.'
During the past year and a half, since the outbreak of the war, the mounted police as a body have rendered magnificent service in the preservation of law and order in Saskatchewan, and, I believe, in the West as a whole. Reference has been made to aliens, or rather to men who are perhaps not aliens but who are naturalized British subjects, although formerly subjects of enemy countries. We have in the West a large number of people who came from Germany, and particularly from Austria. We have had very little trouble with those people in the part of the country from which I come. A number of men have been interned, and a number have been placed on parole by the Northwest Mounted Police. I think some 360 or 370 were interned by the police, and a similar number placed on parole. A number of these came under my personal attention. The total number thus dealt with is very small when compared with the number of these people in Western Canada. I believe, of course, in exercising the greatest vigilance in looking after our alien enemies in this country; but I believe that the mounted police, in (Mr. W. M. Martin.]
our province at least, have done more than any other organization towards keeping these people in order-that is, if there had been any possibility of trouble. I am, of course, more or less inclined to look upon these people who are in this country as being entitled to a certain amount of consideration.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Hear, hear.

I do not believe in dealing out to them what you might term cold justice. I think the mounted police have exercised a reasonable amount of discretion in dealing with them; their justice has been largely tempered with mercy. I have always felt that these people were entitled to a certain amount of consideration largely for this reason, 'that if I myself were residing in Germany or Austria to-day I might be inclined to have my sympathies with the country from which I came, and we cannot expect these people not to have a certain amount of sympathy with their old fatherlands. Bu't, of course, they must be taught to exercise that sympathy in a proper direction. I rose simply for the purpose of expressing my views in regard to the mounted police. I have nothing to say with regard to them except a word of commendation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Registrars of alien enemies are appointed in any part of Canada where representations are made to the Government, or wherever the Government obtains any information which seems to justify their appointment. When they are so appointed they are in constant touch with the chief of police and the civil authorities generally with respect to alien enemies in their vicinity. I entirely concur in my hon. friend's expression of appreciation of the work of the Royal Northwest Mounted Police.
At six o'clock, the Committee took recess.
