The Committee resumed at eight o'clock.
Ocean and river service-maintenance and1 repairs to Dominion steamers and ice-breakers, $1,180,000.
Mr. A. K. MA'CLEAN: That seems a very large item.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The increase this year is $55,000, and it is due to the insertion of an amount for the maintenance of the steamer Montmagny, which, it is expected, will be raised and put in commission, after having lain in the bottom of the St. Lawrence since

the 18th September, 1914. When raised, she will be an extra steamer in the service. The cost of maintenance will be $67,500, but we are making the increase $55,000, as we will have a small surplus in respect of the other vessels. The expenditure under this vote in 1914-15 was $995,545.95, and up to the 31st December last it was $828,620.28. We are asking for the same amount as last year, plus the $55,000 for the maintenance of the Montmagny.
Have we the same number of steamers in the service as last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We will have one more when the Montmagny is raised.
Was the steamer which was sold to the Russian Government replaced?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, she was replaced by the Prince Edward Island, which is one of the mail steamers between the island and the mainland.	.
She is a ferry boat?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes, we are operating the car ferryboat. The car ferry service comes under the jurisdiction of the Railway Department, but for this winter's service the car ferry was placed at the disposal of the Department of Marine, and the Department of Marine pays the expenses of the operation of that steamer during this winter.
Has that car ferry boat been successful?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
We are told that it is
giving very good service.
What are the ice-breakers employed by the Government at present?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Montcalm, the Lady Grey, the Stanley and the Prince Edward Island.

Where are they placed for
the purpose of ice-breaking?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The Montcalm and the
Lady Grey are on the river St. Lawrence; the Stanley and Prince Edward Island are on the service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
Would any of them be available for Sydney harbour?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I am afraid not this year, because I do not think we can take either of the boats from the St. Lawrence, and I am also afraid that at the time that Sydney harbour might want attention it would be
impossible to take the boats away from the route [DOT] between Prince Edward Island and the mainland.
Is the increase due to some repairs on the Montmagny?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend will remember that the Montmagny was sunk in a collision on the St. Lawrence nearly two years ago. We have entered into a contract to have her raised for $27,000. The contractors are to place her in the dock of Levis or there will be no payment. It is a case of no cure, no pay. We expect that the boat will be repaired and ready for use by next summer, and it is for the running of the boat that the extra $55,000 has been placed in the Estimates.
This item does not include the naval service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No.
Will the minister give the number of steamers on the ocean and river service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There are twenty-seven: the Aberdeen, Arranmore, Bellechasse, Scout, Brant, Champlain, Dollard, Druid, Estevan, Frontenac, Grenville, Lady Grey, Lady Laurier, Lambton, Prince Edward Island, Lansdowne, Maggie May, Montcalm, the new ice-breaker, Montmagny, Newington, Quadra, Rouville, Shamrock, Simcoe, Stanley and Vercheres.
Is there any revenue from these steamers?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There is from some. The Champlain conducts the ferry service between Murray Bay and River Ouelle and she earns revenue, but most of these are boats from which there is no revenue. The Aberdeen is engaged in the lighthouse and buoy service on the Bay of Fundy; the Arranmore is engaged in the same service in Nova Scotia; the Estevan in the lighthouse and buoy service in British Columbia; the Lady Laurier in the lighthouse and buoy service in Nova Scotia; the Scout is in the Prescott district; the Simcoe is on the Great Lakes; and the Stanley is in the lighthouse and buoy service in Nova Scotia.
What comes within the definition of maintenance?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The upkeep of the crew, coal, oil, and everything else that is neces-saray to keep the boats running.
How many boats were acquired by the Government during the past year.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None by this department.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Is the minister aware that the heating of the Prince Edward's saloon is very poor, and is any attempt being made to remedy it?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The matter has been attended to, and our latest advice, is that the saloon is comfortably heated.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Could the minister give me the names of the officials, and the stewards on the Stanley and the Prince Edward? '

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I remember that the name of the steward on the Stanley is Hill. I do not remember.the name of the steward on the Scout. The Prince Edward belongs to the Department of Railways and Canals, and all officials on that boat are appointed by that department. We simply operate the boat during the winter, and as soon as the winter is over the boat passes under the absolute control of the Department of Railways and Canals.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
Have the trips been
regular this year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.
I see another item for repairing the steamer Montmagny. Why have one item under Ocean and River Service, and another item under Lighthouse and Coast Service?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The item under discussion is for the ordinary maintenance of the steamers. The other item is an extraordinary item, involving the raising of the Montmagny, and for repairs much more expensive than those which might fairly be charged to maintenance.
How many boats have been sold by the department to the Russian Government since the outbreak of war?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Two, the Earl Grey and the Minto.
Have any boats been purchased to take their places?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
No; the car ferry takes
the place of one of the boats.
Ocean and river service-examiners of masters and mates, $16,500.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
This item is required to pay the salaries, travelling expenses, and
[Mr. Hazen.J
rent of offices of the examiners. We asked for the same amount in 1914-15, and spent $12,723.17. For the current year the estimate is $16,500. Up to the 31$t of December we have spent $10,413. In addition to examining candidates for the positions of masters and mates, the examiners are expected to conduct preliminary investigations into wrecks, and to perform such other duties as the department may from time to time assign to them.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Who is the examiner at Charlottetown?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Capt. Alexander Cameron.

The minister intimated last year that he had in mind some changes in the form of examination for masters and mates which would enable captains holding coasting certificate's to take longer voyages than the present law permits them to take. Has the minister worked that idea out?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: My hon. friend has introduced a Bill for the purpose of allowing those who hold coasting certificates to take Longer voyages, and when the Bill comes up I shall be prepared to give the views of the department to the House.

The Bill I introduced does not deal with the examinations; it simply seeks to have the line extended from 5 degrees north latitude to 40 degrees south latitude, in order to enable coasting vessels to go further south than they can at present. That is not the proposal the minister made last year. He proposed a new examination, and the issuing of a different kind of certificate. Does the minister contemplate doing anything along that line?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
To do anything of that
sort we should have to have legislation. What I suggested last year was that in addition to the deep sea certificate, and the coasting certificate, there might be another certificate which I referred to as a limited foreign certificate, enabling captains to go, not only on coasting voyages, but a much further distance than they can at present. The matter has been given some consideration during the recess, and when my hon. friend's Bill comes up I shall be prepared to state just what our matured opinion on the subject is. As my hon. friend has pointed out to the House on several occasions, owing to the limitation

of a coasting certificate, a good many of our vessels have withdrawn from Canadian register. There is also a tendency to register in the United States and Barbados rather than in Canada. I hope that we shall be able to make an arrangement pretty soon which will be quite satisfactory.
Ocean and river service-investigation into wrecks, $12,300.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The sum voted to us for
the current year was $13,400 and up to the 31st of December, we spent only $3,068. Therefore we think we are justified in reducing this vote by $6,100 as compared with the vote for the current year.

Were there many
wrecks last year?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I have a list here of investigations held on wrecks that occurred during the year.
It would be interesting to know how many lives were lost.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The losses in the wrecks
that were investigated by the commissioner in most cases were small. The list, which is quite lengthy, is up to February 7, of this year. In June, the A. W. Perry stranded and was lost. The finding was that the stranding was in consequence of the carelessness and negligence of the master and the court suspended his certificate for six months. The cost of holding that investigation was $125.46. On August 30, the Alexandria was beached by the master owing to the fury of the gale and he was not held to be at fault. On August 13, 14, and 16, there was an investigation into the collision between the Batiscan and the Ben-gore Head. The Batiscan was held to be at fault; the master was suspended for two years, the pilot fined $100, and the pilot of the Bengore Head had his license cancelled. Does my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) wish me to read the whole list?

No.
Ocean and river service-expenses of schools of navigation, $8,000.

Where are these schools
located?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At Halifax, St. John, Quebec, North Sydney, Yarmouth, Collingwood, Kingston and Vancouver. In addition, we pay with this vote $500 a year to Queen's University, and the university provides free
instruction and pays all expenses of lecture rooms, rent, etc.

Who are in charge of
these schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
At Halifax, Captain John
Simmons; at St. John, Captain R. C. Coles; at Quebec, Captain P. L. LaChance; at North Sydney, Captain James Sutherland; at Yarmouth, Captain J. E. Murphy; at Collingwood, Captain Cole; at Kingston, Captain MacMaster; and at Vancouver, Captain Charles Eddie.
Do you make any allowance to the Technical School at Halifax?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: We supplied the equipment at the Technical School at Halifax, and I think we also pay the instructor.

What number of
students were there?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The school at Halifax is
run the whole year around and is well patronized. During the last six months there has been an average daily attendance of eight pupils, and fifty-nine candidates have been examined for certificates during the past ten months.

What number at other
schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
The average attendance at the school at St. John has been three, and fourteen candidates for certificates have been examined during the past ten months. At Quebec the school was not in operation during the summer and autumn months owing to the transfer of the instructor, Captain P. L. LaChance, to the pilot service of the port. The Quebec school was resumed in December, with Captain Napoleon LaChance as instructor, and there has been an average daily attendance of thirteen pupils. The Kingston school was opened on the 14th of December, under the direction of Queens University, with Captain Mac-Master as instructor, and very satisfactory reports have been received respecting this school. The captain examined two candidates for certificates at Kingston on the 3rd instant. During December marine lectures were delivered at Vancouver, Collingwood, North Sydney and Yarmouth by Captains Eddie, 'Cole, Sutherland and Murphy respectively, and there were very fair attendances.
Air. KYTE- What about North Sydney?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Sutherland reports a fair attendance so far this year.
How much money has been paid by the Government to the instructor at North Sydney?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Captain Sutherland receives $250 a year; Captain Murphy, Yarmouth, the same; Captain Cole, at Collingwood, the same.

I would like to see the minister establish branch schools at points along the coast, because trained seamen are very scarce on the coasts of the Maritime Provinces. It is difficult to secure men to man the vessels there, and some people do not care to go into the shipping business owing to the great difficulty in securing masters and mates who have certificates. My idea is that this branch should be run with a little more vigour, and that points might be selected along the coast where there are numbers of young men engaged in fishing, and where schools might be established. For instance, the late minister furnished some apparatus at Canso a few years ago, and the master of the high school there "undertook to teach the boys navigation. In the winter season, after the month of January, the young fishermen are not very busy, and he had a vigorous class of between forty and fifty doing splendid work, about twice as many as in the city of St. John. I venture to say that there are more sailors at Canso who are prepared to attend a school of this kind and compete for certificates than there are at St. John or Halifax.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is the nearest school North Sydney?

The nearest school is
North Sydney, about one hundred miles away. That is a long distance for the boys to go, and North Sydney is an expensive place to live in. You cannot expect these young men to leave their homes, pay their own expenses, and go to a school in these distant places. It will be a very important step in the right direction if the minister will establish schools at points like Lunenburg, where there must be a large number of young men would attend, and also at Canso, and perhaps at Louisburg. Certainly, in Lunenburg and Canso, there are a number of young men who would like the advantage of a training of this kind. I suggested this to the minister before. The expense would not be great. I do not think it would cost more than $400 in each place to establish a school, which would educate these young men.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The expense would not be great if we could get suitable instructors.

I appreciate very much the remarks of my hon. friend from Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair). The minister knows that in Caraquet there is a fleet of a couple of hundred fishing vessels in which some seven or eight hundred young men learn navigation, as it were by instinct, and become as able as any others simply by following their fathers. A school of the class referred to, if established in Caraquet, would certainly have a large number of pupils. If established in Caraquet, the school would have to be carried on in French, because nearly all those who are inclined to the sea in that portion of the province are French Acadians.
What advantage do the students get who attend these schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: They get instruction in the art of navigation.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: What monetary advantage?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: None, they pay their own expenses, but the instruction is free. Then, if they want to get certificates as masters or mates, they can pay the examination fees, and if they are successful certificates are issued. These certificates give the holders of them the right to command vessels.
Are.these examinations held in other places?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Yes.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I endorse the remarks of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) and the hon. member for Gloucester (Mr. Turgeon). In the province of Prince Edward Island there is no such school as is proposed. I brought this matter to the attention of the minister last session. There are a great many young men engaged in fishing in our province, as well as those in other marine occupations, and yet, as the hon. member for Guysborough has said, it is becoming more difficult to find certificated men as masters and mates. Anything that the department can do to increase the number of competent certificated men will be a great advantage to shipping. The need of a school in Charlottetown is shown by the fact that it has been taken up as a private enterprise. The students have not only to pay their own board but pay for their tuition as well. Perhaps the school is not very well equipped. Is equipment given by the department to these schools?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: In addition to these Government schools, there are a number of private schools, some of which have been in operation for years. The policy of the department has always been to interfere as little as possible with these private schools. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Hughes) speaks of the difficulty of finding certificated men, but if he will refer to page 226 of the last report of the Department of Marine he will find a list of certificates of competency issued to masters, mates and sea-going second mates. This list covers eight pages of rather fine print.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: How many masters?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I cannot give the number offhand, but I think the hon. gentleman will be surpised if he consults the list to see how large the number is.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
The claim made by the
minister-which he made last session also- that the policy of the department is not to interefere with private schools, hardly holds good in the case of Prince Edward Island, because the necessity there, as I have pointed out, has long existed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Is there any private school on the Island?	.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Only the one at Charlottetown, and the very existence of that school proves that many wish to get the benefit of this education. I do not want the department to interfere, by establishing a rival school, but a small grant would enable the teacher or teachers in that school to give tuition free, and this would undoubtedly increase the attendance. Those who wish to attend the school at Charlottetown have to leave their homes in Souris, Tignish, Rustico, or other outlying stations, and come to Charlottetown and.pay their board. The minister should take this matter into careful consideration. The province would, I think, be fairly entitled to that much consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I shall have the greatest pleasure in looking into the matter, and if we find a grievance in Prince Edward Island that should be redressed it will be redressed.
It will be a small thing, why not do it now?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I do not know how I might be interfering with private enterprise there.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I can assure the minister that if he follows the course I suggest he will not interfere with private enterprise.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
Perhaps we can do something between this and next year. Two years ago the hon. member for Bonaventure (Mr. Marcil) pointed out the necessity of having a school somewhere along the Baie des Chaleurs or Gaspe coast in Quebec. He made out such a strong case that I told him I would certainly make arrangements during the year to have instruction given there. I did so, and the school was conducted at Carleton, on the Baie des Chaleurs, during December, 1914, and January, February and March, 1915, ninety-six days in all. The average daily attendance was fouT, the maximum attendance six, and the minimum two. The school was fairly successful, four of the pupils passing for masters of tug-boats, and two for masters of passenger tug-boats on the minor inland waters. Owing to the absence of Captain Landry no steps can be taken to open the school this year. We understand that the desire there now is to have a school for the instruction of engineers for steam vessels, and we are considering that.
My hon. friend from Inverness asked where examinations had to be passed. If at any time we find two or three students at any place desiring to take examinations, say on the coast of Nova Scotia, we do not compel them to go to Halifax, but cause the examiner to go to the town where they are. This avoids putting the candidates to expense.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Was the whole amount voted last year used?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: No. Out of a vote of $8,000 we had used, up to December 31, $2,406.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: The minister could certainly take some of that money to implement the school alt Charlottetown and make it more efficient and available for those who wish to take advantage of it. He has the money; I tlhink he is favourably disposed; the cause is a good one, and, as he gave a promise to the hon. member for Bonaventure last year and carried it out, I would ask him to place the province of Prince Edward Island in line with the other provinces.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I have asked the deputy minister to make a special note with regard to Prince Edward Island, and we shall look into the matter. If conditions exist that make it desirable that there should

be a school of navigation on the island, [DOT]there is no reason why one should not be established there. But I think It will be found that the reason there has not been one on the island is that it might conflict with some other school and perhaps interfere with some legitimate business now [DOT]being carried on in Charlottetown.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I am not asking the minister to interfere with the school already established; I only want him to assist that school and make it more efficient and valuable.
If I make my urgent request for Gloucester, may I have the same assurance as has been given to my hon. friend?

If I understood the minister, he said that officers of ships were more numerous than we supposed they were. I would be glad to know if that is the case, because it is a general complaint on the coast that it is almost impossible to secure masters and mates for oceangoing and coasting vessels. How many qualified during the past yeaT in all these schools? Is the list to which the minister referred a list of qualified men; when was that list revised, and can the minister assure us that these men are in the country and are available? Very often when these young men get certificates they go to Gloucester or some other American port and secure ships there.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I did not refer to a general list, but to the number who received, certificates during the year ended 31st March, 1915. It is a long list and will be found at page 226 of the report of the department. 1 do not know how many are available, but there must be a list somewhere showing that.
Has there been any change in the law requiring vessels to carry [DOT]mates? What tonnage must a vessel be [DOT]before she is obliged to carry a licensed or certificated mate?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: There has been no change [DOT]in the law. It is more difficult to get certificated mates than to get certificated masters. The owners of coasting vessels [DOT]have made representations urging that they should not have to carry certificated [DOT]mates. That is a burning question with the owners of vessels.

This matter has been discussed annually on this same vote. As the hon. member for Guysborough says,

there is a great shortage in the supply of masters and mates in the Maritime Provinces, especially in Nova Scotia. During the last several years it has been a common things to have ships detained in ports for days, and sometimes for weeks, owing to their inability to get certificated mates. There may be fundamental reasons for this which the Government cannot euTe. It is a fact that in the Maritime Provinces today there is very little shipping owned, beyond the smaller shipping used in the coasting and fishing trades.
Whatever be the cause, it is not possible in the Maritime Provinces to get the same number of qualified masters and mates as one could find a number of years ago. In recent years, in my own province at least, it has become the practice to transfer the registry of ships from Canada to Trinidad, the Barbados, and other British possessions. I think that probably, to-day, with regard to the greater portion of all shipping in Nova Scotia not engaged in the purely coasting or fishing trade, the registration has been transferred to Trinidad and the Barbados, in order, I understand, to escape the necessity of carrying certificated mates. If these vessel owners can do that, anii escape the necessity of carrying certificated mates, there is not much encouragement to young men who purpose pursuing a marine career to obtain their certificates. I think it is also difficult to obtain certificated masters and there is also a great shortage in that respect. I do not object to the establishment of these small schools at any point which needs them. So far they have not been successful. I remember that when I represented the county of Lunenburg a school was started there. For a few weeks there was a very considerable attendance, but in a short, time the school proved a failure and I do not think it has since been resuscitated. That is true regarding a great many other ports in the province. I have frequently said here before that a better way of interesting young men and providing training for a marine career would be to have one central school, where a great number of young men might congregate together, and from the contact and association they would receive new views and wider ambitions. The great trouble about the small school is that the attendance is limited and the advantages are not very great. I remember a number of years ago men Goming from all parts of the province to attend a

private school at Halifax wliich was in existence when I was at college there. I do not think the expense is any impediment whatever to young men desirous of attending these schools.
A likely attendant at a marine school is one who has had some service at sea and he is not the sort of person who is apt to complain about the small cost of attending the school. I do not agree with some of the views presented by my hon. friend from Kings, P.E.I. (Mr. Hughes), because you cannot make a marine school with persons who object to making some sort of expenditure towards acquiring his education. I would hardly approve of that, although I should thoroughly approve of assisting a school in any way one possibly could. It may be that the difficulty in getting, in the Maritime Provinces, a sufficient supply of certificated masters and mates is due to our shipping laws of one kind or another and our statutory requirements in respect to masters and mates. Practically all the vessels from western Nova Scotia are registered in Barbados and Trinidad, but if you could avoid that and secure the registration of these vessels at home ports, you might be able to supply the ambition of our young men. This is a matter that requires looking into.

To what extent are these
certificates recognized by the Board of Trade in England?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
They are recognized by
the Board of Trade absolutely. My hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) asked me a question as to the tonnage of a vessel engaged in the coasting trade that had to obtain a certificated master and mate. A ship of 150 tons has to have a certificated master to engage in the coasting trade, while a ship of 400 tons and upwards is required to have a certificated master and also a certificated mate.

In reference to what my hon. friend from Halifax (Mr. Maclean) has said, really the main reason why vessels are being transferred to Barbados and other colonies is because they are not allowed to clear for distant ports. Most of these vessels over 400 tons require to have masters and mates. The owners of these vessels do not send them to sea without these officers. But the main reason why they seek registration elsewhere is that the customs officer will not allow them to go to
distant places. If a man comes
9 p.m. to clear for the River Plate the Canadian customs officer will tell him that he cannot allow him to go farther than the fifth degree of north latitude. The River Plate at present happens to be the place where the best business is to he obtained, and, therefore, these owners are driven to Barbados to register their ships. I do not want to enter into this question just now. When my Bill is before the House I will give the minister the reasons I have for asking him-to adopt it as a Government measure, which I hope he will do this year.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: I cannot see the force of the reasoning of my hon. friend from Halifax. I think he favours the establishment of a large school at Halifax.
Oh, no.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Or at some point in Nova Scotia, but he would not have one at Charlottetown.
Oh, yes.
I think it was St. John that he had in mind.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext:
That appears strange to
me. I do not see why. The very fact that there is a school at Charlottetown without any assistance shows the advantage and necessity of such an institution. I could not present any stronger argument than that. There must surely be a necessity for it when private enterprise tries to meet the necessity. If the department is encouraging such schools in the other provinces it seems to me that it would be a wise thing to encourage a school where it has already been established and where the facts of its establishment prove the advantage of it. There is another point but I do not know that the time is opportune to discuss it. I, and I presume other hon. members from the Maritime Provinces, get letters from coasting captains and owners complaining of the'privileges that are given to Norwegian and foreign vessels engaged in the coasting trade. They say that our men are at a very great disadvantage. If we buy a vessel, for instance, in Norway, or in any part of the world, and bring it here we have to pay a duty of from 25 to 33 per cent. But the Norwegians can come here in their own vessels. I understand that they fit them out in Norway, where provisions are much cheaper than they are in Canada; they are manned by Norwegians, and the

wages are much lower than in Canada. They come here and are admitted to all the coasting privileges of this country. They carry cargoes from one port to another, competing with our sea-faring men, with the result that complaints are loud and long. I presume that the department is cognizant of these complaints, and perhaps we might as well discuss this matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The matter falls within the control of the Customs Department and not the Marine Department. For a good' many years, since 1904, there has been passed from year to year a regulation allowing vessels of not less than 2,000 tons, owned by Norwegians, and trading between the Maritime Province ports and the ports of Quebec and Montreal, to engage in that business. I am not very familiar with the subject, but I think the regulation was passed for the purpose of enabling the coal owners of Nova Scotia to get their coal to the Montreal market. I have been told, and I think there is a report to that effect, that, if it were not for that privilege accorded to the Norwegians, the coal could not be brought in sufficient quantities to Montreal every year, and the result would be that American coal would have to be brought in to a greater extent than at present to supply the markets of Montreal and the West. The regulation applies, I think, only to vessels over 2,000 tons.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Not to smaller vessels?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Only to vessels of 2,000 tons and upwards.

The point raised by the hon. member for Kings has suggested another matter to my mind. Whatever there may be in the objection raised to Norwegian shipping, I feel it would be hardly fair to press that objection at the present time, because Canada is suffering from a shortage of shipping in the province of Nova Scotia. There is really a coal famine in many parts of the province, despite the fact that we live in a province no part of which is far removed from a coal field, and that is due to a lack of shipping.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I understand it was partly due to a shortage of miners in Cape Breton.

it was due to the great demand for coal, and to the fact that it was impossible to obtain sufficient shipping. There is a coal famine in the Island of Newfoundland because it is impossible to get shipping. I have in mind a place west of Halifax where the people 
were obliged to do absolutely without coal during the present winter. If the coal was available at the collieries, the shipping was not available, and the coal could not be taken there by rail. This condition is very liable to recur next year, because the demand for coal will be greater than the capacity of the mines to supply it. The available shipping will not be greater, but in all likelihood it will he less. Is it not possible that this fleet of steamers, to maintain which we pay $1,250,000, could be available in the fall of the year, after the services .of the department have been completed, for the carriage of coal to certain sections of the country. I do not know whether that is practicable. It may be that the department is allowing steamers to lie in the River St. Lawrence all winter that could be made useful, perhaps not for the purpose I have mentioned, but for other purposes. There is a tremendous shortage of shipping in the Maritime Provinces during all seasons of the year. At all events, that was the ease last year, and I believe it will be more severe next year. If there are any ships of the Marine Department laid up in the river St. Lawrence during the winter, could they not he transferred to -the Maritime Provinces late in the fall, so as to have them available if needed.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I do not think that any of these vessels would be suitable for carrying coal. As my hon. friend knows, they are not large vessels; they have been built for the purpose of putting out and taking up buoys, taking supplies to the different lighthouses, and doing that class of work. I doubt whether any of them are capable of being used as colliers. There are not many of them lying in the St. Lawrence. Take the Arramore, for instance. That boat is in Halifax during the winter months doing work in that neighbourhood, and most of our boats are well employed. They have to be repaired and overhauled annually, and as a rule they are kept pretty busy. For coal carrying purposes large dead weight boats are necessary. Some of the Government vessels carry coal to the lighthouses, but I do not think they could relieve the situation to which my hon. friend refers. If I understand him correctly, his view agrees with the idea that in order to get the coal away from the Nova Scotia ports to the ports of the St. Lawrence it is necessary to allow these Norwegian vessels to carry it. If that ser-

vice were cut off, there would be a shortage of the coal supply in Montreal, and the price would advance-

There is a difference ot opinion about that. My own view is that this is not the proper time to press the objection raised by the hon. member for Kings, because the coal companies of Nova Scotia have great difficulty in supplying the demands along the St. Lawrence. In fact they cannot do it, and I am afraid they will not be able to do it for several years. Has the Government had under consideration during the past year the idea of supplying some marine tonnage in Canada, or of encouraging it by advancing money for the construction of vessels or otherwise? Canadian trade is liable to suffer immensely in the future by reason of lack of tonnage. The destruction of the world's tonnage during the past 18 months has been enormous, and it will probably be at least ten years before the tonnage destroyed can be restored. In Canada we depend entirely upon the exports of the products of the mines, the forests, the sea and the land. We cannot import anything unless we export, and it is absolutely necessary that we should he secured in the possession of tonnage sufficient to carry these exports. The minister has already stated that he has made arrangements with the Admiralty to secure tonnage, particularly for the carriage of munitions of war.
France has undertaken to advance money to persons who are willing to buy ships, or to have them constructed, and I think the Government of Canada might do well to consider giving assistance of this kind. I do not know what conditions are like on the Pacific, but there is no doubt at all that a certain extra amount of tonnage on the Atlantic might be the salvation of Canadian trade. But this must not be left till too late; it must be done at the proper time. I should like to hear from the minister whether the Government has had this matter under consideration.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
I know my hon. friend would not expect me to tell him in detail just what has been discussed in connection with this matter between the members of the Cabinet. I may say, however, that the subject to which he refers has received the very serious consideration and attention of the Government. There are certain difficulties in the way, however. My hon. friend is no doubt right in saying that we may, suffer in the future from lack of tonnage.
That is true of all countries in the world.
I am told that a very unfortunate state of affairs exists at present in Australia and New Zealand on account of the difficulty they have in getting ships to carry away the wool, and it is not only unfortunate for Australia and New Zealand, but for the other countries that use the wool, and for ' the countries whose mills manufacture it.
I may say that since I spoke on this subject during the debate on the Address the Admiralty have furnished us with. more transports. At the present time fifty-three transports are assigned to the Atlantic trade. I get returns every morning, and I find that nearly every morning there are six or seven transports at Halifax, and five, six or seven at St. John-usually from twelve to fourteen boats at the two ports. At the present moment those transports are taking away Canadian goods-munitions of war, hay, oats, etc.-as fast, and I am inclined to think a little faster than the railways are able to get them to the ports of Halifax and St. John. At the present f,ime, therefore, there is little disturbance of Canadian trade on account of lack of tonnage, but I quite agree that disturbance may come in the future. There is, of course, a great deal less tonnage than before the war broke out. Many ships have been either destroyed, interned, or assigned to naval purposes. In regard to my hon. friend's suggestion that people should be encouraged to increase the tonnage of our country, I may say that at the present time people are not disposed to put their money very largely into ships. The expense of building is very great and the cost of the raw material is very high. On the otheT hand, freights are exceedingly high, but there is great uncertainty how long that may continue. Of course, I am not in a position to give any detailed statement to the House on this question, but I may say that negotiations have been going on, and much correspondence has taken place.

Perhaps my hon. friend can tell us how it is that Japan is going ahead with enormous rapidity in the building of a mercantile marine. All the shipyards in Japan, the newspapers inform us, are busy night and day turning out ships. Thousands of men are engaged in the work. But here in Canada, with vast supplies to send across the Atlantic, we are doing 'absolutely nothing 'along that line. Our people, I regret to siay, are receiving absolutely no, encouragement from the Govern-

ment to go on with ship building. Friamce has given encouragement, with a view to increasing her mercantile marine for the purpose of enabling products of other countries to be brought to France more cheaply than would otherwise be the case. To-day the people of Canada, and those who consume Canadian goods, are paying on an average one thousand per cent more [DOT] than what is reasonable-one thousand per cent more than was paid before the war broke out.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is true of other countries besides Canada.

But, other countries are trying to make good the deficiency. They are trying to build up a carrying trade themselves. Japan is doing wonderful work in that direction. Here in Canada it seems to me that our mercantile marine is simply going to destruction; it is gradually growing less and less, and no encouragement at all is being given.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The main trouble is that our regular lineis on the Atlantic and Pacific have been commandeered by the Admiralty.
They are not Canadian ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Canadian Pacific Railway-
Those are British ships.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: But they are owned in Canada.

They are built under circumstances and under laws which give to the British shipbuilder an enormous advantage over the Canadian shipbuilder. Those ships enter our ports without paying any duty. They come into Canada without paying one single cent into the treasury. On the other hand, a shipbuilder in Canada must pay an enormous duty on a vast number of articles . which go into the building of ships. If a Canadian shipbuilder wants to build a sailing vessel and operate it by means of auxiliary power, be has to pay an enormous duty on the machinery required to secure that power.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The Canadian shipbuilder gets a large rebate on most of the material that goes into the construction of a ship. Does my hon. friend suggest that we should place a duty on ships from Great Britain- ships that come here flying the British flag?	I | ,:

Gentlemen on this side of the House might hesitate to advocate general protection, but surely hon. gentle. men opposite, who impose a very high protective duty against almost every other class of people in Canada, ought not to hesitate to give some encouragement to the building of ships in this country. One would think it would not be straining their conscience too much, or trespassing too much on their good judgment, if they were to move along these lines. As a representative of a Maritime province, I desire to say that there is no interest in Canada which is more deserving of encouragement than ship building. It would probably not be necessary to impose a very heavy duty, but surely it would not be unreasonable for the Government to give some encouragement by way of a bonus to encourage the building of ships. It is not absolutely necessary to go into the building of steel ships. Wooden vessels could be constructed, and would be able to do good work in the carrying trade. My hon. friend says the matter is under consideration. He makes , the same objection that the Minister of Trade and Commerce made the other day, namely, that the war may end very suddenly,' and that the people are not willing to go into this business. Should an argument like that influence the Government of this country? Surely it is of enormous importance that Canadian products-Canadian wheat, Canadian cattle, Canadian pulp and lumber-should be taken across the Atlantic and to our allies as cheaply as possible, and that this enormously heavy rate, which is a thousand times greater than it ought to be, should be done away with. Yet the Government, although the war has been going oh now for about eighteen months, has done absolutely nothing and the minister tells this committee just what the Minister of Trade and Commerce stated the other night, that the matter is under consideration, but that there are serious difficulties in the way. This Government should go ahead in the wiay of encouraging shipbuilding irrespective of whether this war may last for one year or for ten years. They should look ahead and seek to relieve the-situation by fostering a shipbuilding industry in Canada. There are splendid opportunities on both oceans; we have plenty of men who understand everything about shipbuilding; we have some of the finest ship-carpenters in the world, and we know that, in the past, when we were building wooden ships, the ships of Canada were found on every sea and bore the palm away from the

ships of any other country. If there was sufficient encouragement we could build ships in Canada, and now is the time when we may reasonably look forward to this as there will be an enormous demand for shipping for a good many years to come. We ought to take hold of the matter seriously and see if shipbuilding cannot be so encouraged that it may be undertaken in earnest on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts. I do not mention this simply with the idea of bringing my views before the House in order to get them on Hansard, but I do it most sincerely and earnestly in the hope that my hon. friend who presides over the Department of Marine and Fisheries, which is peculiarly charged with this matter, who represents a maritime constituency and a city which used to be one of the great shipowninig cities in the world; a city where they used to build ships by the score and by the hundred, may take it up and press it upon his colleagues, and see that some action is taken in the immediate future, so that we may not come back next session and be told that the matter is still under consideration and that there are still difficulties in the way.

I fear we never
can become a great shipbuilding country while we have the present tariff fates, because so long as Brutish shipbuilders can build ships from 35 to 50 per cent below what we can construct them for in Canada, there is very little prospect for the construction of ships in Canada to any great extent. Further, I think the ownership of shipping and engagement in shipping is preliminary to the construction of ships in any country. The important thing, however, for Canada to-day is to own ships and this would be a very opportune time to encourage the early acquisition of shipping and that can be helped by removing the duty, which I understand is 25 per cent, Canadian interests might buy some ships abroad from neutral nations during the next few years and if that is possible, there is no reason in the world why a tariff of 25 or 35 per cent should be imposed. We want some changes in the tariff immediately to encourage the purchase of ships.

In the remarks of the
two hon. gentlemen who have just preceded me we have an example of that delightful unanimity which prevails so frequently on the other side of the- House. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugs-ley) almost announced himself as a protectionist 'along shipbuilding lines, while the hon, junior member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean) considers that an impossibility, under existing conditions of shipbuilding in the old land with which we could not expect to compete. However, it was not to criticise the remarks of these two hon. gentlemen that I rose to speak. Speaking entirely for myself, because this is a forum where I presume we have the right to express our own viewis whether they have any value or not, I cannot see any reason why a country like Canada, which owns railway lines like the Intercolonial, which takes the money of the country to equip and operate those lines, should not also own and operate steamship lines. The difficulty of the transportation of wheat from the West to the markets of the world would be largely overcome if the Government would spend some millions of dollars in building and operating lines of wheat freighters which would guarantee to the farmers of the West that their wheat would be carried to the markets of the world at the lowest possible cost. Not only would we be justified in doing that by reason of the benefit that would accrue to the growers of wheat in the West, but it would necessarily mean that, instead of about 40 per cent of our surplus wheat leaving Canada by Canadian ports and the other 60 per cent by American ports, a very much larger proportion would go over Canadian railways to Canadian ports. I agree with the remarks of the hon. junior member for Halifax. I believe this is the time when we should boldly launch out towards owning our own ships, and spend a large amount of money, if necessary, in building vessels to carry our produce across the ocean. The United States has never been a maritime country; it has never purchased a large merchant marine and it does not look as if it ever would, and after this war is over, it seems to me there is going to be a magnificent opportunity for Canada to launch out into something big along the lines of a merchant marine. As a man from one of the older provinces, I believe that the country would be warranted in taking steps along that line. It seems to me that the result would be wonderfully advantageous to the producers of wheat in the Western provinces.

This problem is not one for the Maritime Provinces, it is really a national problem. Every acre of land that is brought under cultivation

in the West, and every additional hundred bushels of wheat produced, makes greater the necessity for action in regard to this matter. Of what use to us as a nation are the three great transcontinental lines now practically in operation from sea to sea if, when we reach the seaboard on the Atlantic or the Pacific, there is no tonnage to carry our products except what is 'beyond the control of the Canadian people? When our friends in the West, of both political parties, say that grievances exist; that there is discrimination in ocean freights; and that the Western farmers have suffered because of the failure to transport products, there can be no manner of doubt that there is some basis for what they say. But I am not sure that our friends from the West quite grasp the situation as it exists in the Maritime Provinces. Thirty-five years ago, the foreign trade of Canada was almost exclusively carried by ships owned and built in Canada. Before the decay of the industry in wooden vessels, the tonnage of Canada upon the sea was greater per capita than that of lany nation in the world1-greater than that of England herself. After the disappearance of wooden vessels, there came an interim in which 'the carrying trade fell largely into the bands of Great Britain andi Norway. The Norwegians purchased the old Canadian wooden vessels, and by rigid lowering of expenses were able to operate them at rates below those asked by others. Now the question arises whether our internal development is to be hampered and interfered with by the possibility of lack of tonnage on the sea. That condition arose quite apart from the war. Last year we had an abnormally large crop, but even if the war had not interfered, as it has to a great degree, with the handling of that crop upon the ocean, there would be discontent and trouble probably just the same. Every year, as our production increases, there is great discontent in Canada over this question. Now, we have three propositions in this matter. The proposition of the hon. member for Prontenac (Mr. Edwards) is that Canada should own and control a mercantile marine. That is very similar to the proposition advanced by President Wilson last year in the message to the United States Senate, in which he proposed that the nation should purchase a very large number of vessels as a means of solving the problem which exists in that country. That proposition did not pass the 
Congress of the United States. The tremendous extent of our territory, and the fact that the greater number of our people are not familiar with maritime affairs, surrounds the question with a great many difficulties, as the Minister of Marine and Fisheries will see. When the hon. member for Halifax (Mr- Maclean) speaks of Canada owning a mercantile marine, I take it, he does not speak of it in the same sense as does the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards). What he means is that Canadians individually should develop and own a mercantile marine. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Maclean) points out that on account of tariff conditions there are difficulties in the way of vessel construction. The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), as I understand him, proposes to solve the problem by giving a bonus to those who will engage in the building of ships in Canada. These three honourable gentlemen, like everyone in Canada who has considered this problem, realize its significance and the necessity of some solution being found. We have been going on for twenty-five years considering whether we should subsidize this railway or bonus that one, until we have a great network of railways throughout Canada. But these will be of no value if their freights cannot be taken beyond the shores of Canada. That something must be done is recognized. I hope the Government will not deal with this question by appointing a commission to look into it. These commissions to deal with matters that the Government itself ought to deal with do not facilitate progress. The problem can be solved, and solved in the interests of the Canadian people. I come from a constituency in which steel vessels have been built without ,a bonus and in spite of tariff difficulties. At this moment you cam build vessels in Canada of steel, equal to those which come from the Clyde. We forget that the only reason why we did not begin to build steel vessels to replace the wooden vessels twenty-five years ago is that we had no steel industry in Canada. At that time we had no industry that could roll a steel rail or east a steel ingot, much less roll steel plates for building vessels. It is only within the 'last ten or fifteen years that that industry has arisen. Today we have many places where steel plates are rolled. Once you have the -steel plates the matter of putting them together is a very small problem. The proposition is one that requires consideration and the in-

auguration of a policy on broad lines. If there are conditions in the tariff which prevent development of the industry, amend the tariff. Let us not bandy words about our old differences with regard to free trade and protection, but come down to practical lines and assist in the establishing of an industry that is absolutely essential. We talk of the prosperity of the steel industry in this country. Why is it prosperous? Simply because the mills are rolling steel ingots' to be turned into shells, while another shop takes that ingot and carries on the manufacture to the completion of the article in the form of a shell. But some day this shell production is going to stop, and when it stops the steel industry of this country will have nothing to do so far as one can see under existing conditions. The construction of the transcontinental railway lines provided employment for the men engaged in the steel business for a long period of years. We cannot look forward to further large railway construction. The men engaged in 'the steel industry in this country will tell you that they are prepared to roll the steel necessary for the construction of vessels. Some plan ought to be devised by this Government-and I am not speaking at all in a spirit of partisanship-that would remove the existing difficulties, the nature of which could easily be ascertained upon inquiry, providing for the disappearance from the tariff of those things that interfere with the industry, and providing, by a bonus if you will, as is done in other countries, for the inauguration of the building of vessels. The question is one which can not be settled haphazard, but the Government, or any minister devoting his time and attention to it, could develop a policy within a very short time which would mean that something could be done to create in Canada a steel shipbuilding industry and bring about the construction of vessels which are absolutely essential to the future of Canada.
. This discussion is one which has taken a wide range, but the opportunity has not come hitherto this session, and I think that, the question having been discussed along this line, every hon. gentleman can see that the situation which exists is one that ought to be remedied. Let me reiterate this fact, that the condition is not one which has been precipitated by the war. Those of us who live down by the sea, when we see vessels going out from our ports, know that if this war had never occurred the difficulty would 45
have existed just the same, and that it h.is been increasing year by year. We know that the revenues of the Minister of Railways and Canals have been diminished in the past because there have been no vessels to take tthe products carried over the Government road. The situation as put by the hon. member for Frontenac (Mr. Edwards) is absolutely correct. Millions of tons of Canadian products and freight pass through American seaports, and have been passing for the last ten or fifteen years in increasing quantities, simply because Canada has stood still on the question of marine construction. That condition will continue increasingly to exist, and will become very much more acute unless the Government deal with the question. The Minister of Railways and Canals is interested in this problem quite as much as the Minister of Marine is. We have two great transcontinental railway systems passing through Canadian territory, and we are looking for the time when the other will find an outlet through Canadian territory to the Atlantic, just as it already has to the West, and, as a patriotic people, we are hoping for the time when Canada will send her own products over her own roads down to the seaboard, ship them through our own ports, and carry them in our own bottoms across the sea.
Canada can never reach the point which we are all so ambitious to see her attain; she will never have that forceful place in the Empire, until we show that at our own steel works we can do what the men in the Clyde are doing, until we show to the whole world that we can do that which any other part of the British Empire can do. I have heard h,on. gentlemen tell us that you cannot do this because they are doing it in some other country. Everybody in these strenuous times is beginning to realize that we Canadians do not need to take off our hats to the men of any other nation or of any other part of the Empire whether it is in fighting or in industry. Canadians can do anything in an industrial way that is done by any other nation. Who would have thought a year and a half ago that every wheel in every iron shop in this country would be turning, that every lathe would be at work, producing shells for the war? Did anybody think that we could produce shells? Yet all of our industries are busy, all our workmen are engaged day by day at that industry. They told us that we could not make shells in 1914 and some people say that we cannot build ships. The



men who are turning out shells to-day can produce the steel plates that are used in the construction of modern steel ships, and they can rivet these plates together just as well as men who happened to be bom on the banks of the Clyde, or at Newcastle-on-Tyne, or anywhere in France or Germany.
Look at the question in the broad way, and what is the problem? You can assist or impede the development of an industry by questions of tariff and by other elements which must be taken into consideration. You must remember also that the inauguration of an industry has to take place. It is insulting to the intelligence and the capacity of our people to say that we cannot do this, because we can. All the rest is a matter of governmental action and governmental assistance along such lines as experience and wisdom may dictate. Let the Government devote their energy, attention and ability to the consideration of this whole question so that they may be in a position to formulate a policy which they can place before the Canadian people entirely apart from anything like narrow or partisan lines. I feel satisfied that the Government that would propound such a policy would receive the support of all patriotic Canadians irrespective of party.	'[DOT]

I quite agree with
some of the remarks made by my hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), and with that one in particular to the effect that all the money that we have put into railways during past years, amounting to probably over one thousand ' million dollars, will be, to a large extent, unproductive, unless some better system of handling the crops that these railways handle shall be adopted in the future than in the past. I would like to point out that the excess freight rates charged on the 1915 crop of wheat grown in western Canada will amount to between 340,000,000 and $50,000,000, and that for carrying the wheat across the water, it will cost between $30,000,000 and $40,000,000 this year more than it would have cost previous to the war. Even if it costs something to secure a proper supply of bottoms to take the products of Canada across the water we can afford to pay something to have that done. But the question really resolves itself into what is the best way of handling this problem. Last year when the matter of granting a new charter to the Canadian Pacific Steamship Company-a subsidiary company to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, the vessels all being owned by the Can-
[Mr. Macdonald. 1
adian Pacific railway-was up, some of us endeavoured to have the Government take power to control the rates on these vessels. The Minister of Railways could not see it in that light; he could not see that he had any power to control the rates on the ocean. It seems very strange to me that if the Canadian Pacific railway can carry wheat from the western provinces to Montreal, St. John, or Halifax at the same rate that they charged two or three years ago, it should be necessary, the moment that wheat. strikes tide water this year, for them to charge five, six and seven times as much as they did previously. How are we going to get a remedy? Is it going to be by following the suggestion of my hon. friend from St. John (Mr. Pugsley), that the Canadian Government could build and own the ships, or by following the suggestion of my hon. friend from Pictou that subsidies should be granted to secure the building of ships, or by so arranging the tariff that the ships will be built? I do not know which of these proposals would be the best, but I want to say that in the United States, under a heavy protective tariff, they have struggled for the last fifty years to build ships, and, they have not done it, and can not do it. My idea is that if you want to build ships to carry the grain products of Canadian farms from this continent to the European market, you do not have to build Government ships, and you do not have to pay a great big bonus to the Canadian Pacific railway or to the Allan line or to any otheT company, to build ships. You do not have to give great big subsidies to the steamship lines. What you want to do is to take the duties off the products, to make the building of ships cheap, to follow the example of Great Britain. How does Great Britain manage to have such fleets on every one of the seven seas? Simply because she frames her own laws so that the ships can be built cheaply and run cheaply. We in Canada have followed the opposite course and now we are up against a wall, and a remedy must be found. I do not know how that remedy will be found, but I am absolutely satisfied that the best remedy that could be found would be to take off the duties, to make the' material that goes into your ships cheap, and then you would find, as the hon. member for Pictou said, that you have the men in Canada, that there is the money in Canada, that would produce these ships and carry the produce of the country to the markets of the world

at a proper price, so that the farmer would get a reasonable price for growing the products. To my mind that would be a much better way than either to build Government ships or to subsidize privately owned ships. If you build Government ships, and I think we can build them-I do not at all agree with the Prime Minister when he said that we could not build ships in Canada in fifty years. We can build them to-day and to-morrow.

The Prime Minister
never said anything of the kind.
I sat in the House of Commons and heard the Prime Minister say in 1911-12 that you could not build a navy in Canada in 25 or 50 years.
That is entirely different from your first position. You were in power for fifteen years and did not make much of a start at them.
You are a small Canadian.

We can build ships in Canada to-day, and we have
10 p.m. proven it time and again. We have built ships on the Great Lakes, some of them larger than many that cross the ocean, and we would build them to-day if the tariff was so arranged that they could be built profitably. Why are they not built? Simply because it is not profitable to build them.
Where would you get the material?

I understand from the
hon. member for Pictou that they can roll plates and all sorts of steel that goes into a ship down in Nova Scotia. My hon. friend comes from a province very close to Nova Scotia and he may have heard that there is an iron and steel works in Sydney.

The hon. member said that the United States does not build its ships and never will. They produce everything which goes into a ship. Why then are they not able to build the ships as well as in England?

I told the hon. gentleman why they have not been able to do so. It is 'because they have a high protective tariff and the ships cost so much that they cannot compete with Great Britain with her low tariff.

But they produce
everything that goes into the ship, and

They produce everything that goes into the ship, but the tariff on the material going into the ship is so high that it enables the home manufacturer to charge a price which makes the completed ship cost so much that it cannot carry freight at a profit. And that accounts to a large extent for our not having ships. Then the United States coasting laws prohibit foreign ships from coming in and carrying freight from one port to another. That accounts for the United States not having a mercantile marine and it accounts for Canada not having a proper mercantile marine. We built ships when wooden ships were in vogue, and now that steel ships are altogether in use we could make steel ships; but you have to make the conditions such that men with capital will see a fair return for the capital if they put it into ships.
