speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The question is navigation schools.

I know, but the hon.
gentleman took this opportunity of discussing the general question, and now we are discussing the question of ships, which has something to do with navigation, and navigation schools have something to do with training officers for the ships- We must have the ships. We must have some better methods than we have to-day for carrying the products of the Canadian farm across to the . markets of the world. The question is how best to accomplish that. That is not for me to decide, but for hon. gentlemen on the Government benches. The Minister of Railways last year would not agree to control the freight rates on the ocean vessels. Now, since he would not agree to do that, and this year the prices are up five hundred fold and more, I think it is up to my hon. friends the Minister of Railways and the Minister of Marine, if they will not agree to control the rates on the ocean, to devise some other method by which the products of the Canadian farm can be put on the markets of the world without having to pay two, or three, or four, or five, or six times an ordinary freight rate. Until we can do that we will not have accomplished our duty, in this House. We are here to legislate for the people of Canada, and, speaking for one class alone, the wheat growers, the farmers of the three Prairie provinces, I say that this year they will pay over $40,000,000 more than the ordinary freight rate for the shipment of their grain across the water. If that is the case, if on one crop we pay an extra $40,000,000, that calls for a remedy of some kind; and it is up t,o the gentlemen sitting on the treasury benches to provide some better method than exists at present for getting the Canadian crop to the markets of the world.

Some time ago I had the honour of attending a banquet of master shipbuilders and master mariners

on the Great Lakes, and the shipbuilders' complaint was that they had not any protection in Canada, with the result that the ship building industry had not proceeded along progressive lines commensurate with the general prosperity of the country. I think we must ail agree that in future years the great prosperity of Canada will depend largely on its export of its agricultural products, and when we consider that this year we had something 'like 376,000,000 bushels of wheat grown in the great Northwest and that sixty per cent of that was shipped by other than Canadian vessels, I think it does indicate that we should take some stepS towards a regeneration of our ocean traffic- Something like one thousand million bushels of wheat and coarse grains were grown in the West this year. What is the use of our having a hopper of that dimension in the Northwest, filled with grain which we cannot consume in this country, unless we have a spout sufficiently large to take care of it? That spout, it seems to me, must be enlarged either by granting bonuses to encourage ship building or by building ships for ourselves, or in some other way increasing the freight accommodation on the ocean.
There is another point in connection with that, and it is that we have, practically speaking, no control over the rates on wheat or other agricultural products from Canada to Great Britain. While we have control over the rates on the railways, we have no control over the through rate; we have no control over rates outside the Dominion of Canada. If we had the control, either by ownership, or by a subsidy, we would virtually have control of the wheat from the great western country to the British market. As you all know, the consumption of wheat in Great Britain this year amounts to something like 485,000,000 bushels. I see no reason why we should not supply every part of that demand, because we are nearer to Great Britain than the Argentine Republic. The freight rate from the Argentine to Great Britain js about 80 cents, while it is 35 cents or 40 cents from Canada. We should, therefore, take advantage of the shorter distance, and there is no reason why we should not supply the greater part, if not all, of the wheat required in Great Britain. I do not know- whether my hon. friend from Assini-boia (Mr. Turriff) is .quite accurate when he speaks of $40,000,000 that could be saved. It may be so, because we have a product of 367,000,000 bushels of wheat, and while we will not export it all, nevertheless the price

of the wheat will be determined by our ability to export our surplus. If we have 367,000,000 bushels in Canada, and increase the price 10 cents, by extra facilities on the ocean that would be a saving of $37,000,000. These figures warrant us in at least attempting to make some provision for our great export in the future. In times of peace we are told we should prepare for war, and in times of war we should prepare for peace. We are expecting a great influx of immigrants after the war is over. Perhaps we will not have such a large influx as some people imagine, because I believe that in the reconstruction of Europe after the war a great many people will be required. Besides, we will not have so many able-bodied men in the country then as we have to-day. Nevertheless, it is admitted by the statesmen of Great Britain that there will be considerable emigration. I noticed that Mr. Bonar Law, in a recent speech, said that there would naturally be a great influx of immigrants to Canada after the war. For the reasons I have submitted, I think it is imperative upon the Government to take some steps along the line of increasing the facilities for exporting our agricultural products. My hon. friend from Assiniboia stated that the United States were not able to build steamships in competition with Great Britain. I understand there is a Bill now before Congress granting $50,000,000 for the purpose of assisting shipbuilding. My hon. friend also stated that the reason why ships were not built in Canada was/because they could not be built as cheaply as elsewhere. If it is not profitable to build ships in Canada, then the only way in which to make it profitable is to give some encouragement.
Take the duties off.

You cannot take the duties off, because British ships can come in, but you can give protection to the shipbuilding industry just the same as to any other industry. I do not know which would be the better way, whether to build the ships ourselves and put them on the ocean, thereby regulating the traffic, or whether to give a subsidy; but if we can increase the facilities, increase the capacity of the spout I am certain we will go a long way towards solving the difficulties which the farmers experience in the West.
My hon. friend seems to speak with authority and knowledge. He said that we might control rates by subsidizing the vesse ,s. Did I understand him ter say that?
Yes.

Well, then, will my hon. friend explain how it is that the steamship lines which to-day are receiving a very large subsidy from this Government-one company receiving as much as $1,000,000 a year-are, as I am informed, charging the same high rates as the unsubsidized companies, and are allowed iby the Government to do so.

The conditions to/
day are abnormal over the whole world. They are paying 80 cents a bushel for taking wheat from the Argentine to Liverpool, while we are paying 40 cents a bushel from Canada. The conditions are abnormal because of the scarcity of ships due to the war, and to the fact that many ships are engaged on behalf of the Admiralty.

But does not my hon.
friend see that the very object, or what ought to be the object, of subsidizing a line of steamers from Canada would be to ensure reasonable rates at all times? What is there to warrant these steamship companies which receive a subsidy from this Government, in the case of one company to the extent of $1,000,000 ia year, raising their rates from $800 to $1,000 per cent, or to warrant this Government permitting them to do so?

My hon. friend
knows quite well that the subsidy which is granted to these steamship companies is not for the purpose of facilitating the carriage of freight, but to facilitate the carriage of mail, and the subsidy is comparatively small. That is not the kind of subsidy to which I refer. I have in mind a substantial subsidy to ocean-going ships that would enable us to control the rates upon freight of all kinds, and particularly upon wheat.

This is such an important discussion that to enable all those who desire to speak upon it, members will have to express their views briefly. It is really the greatest question that is before the Canadian people to-day. I have no faith in Government-owned steamships. I do not believe that the traffic would be satisfactorily handled by steamships owped by the Government. My hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Middlebrol mentioned that the condition on the freight market today is abnormal, and that is true. When you

go back a few years you find that the -rates for carrying wheat from Montreal were practically down to five cents a bushel, and at New York the rate was about one penny half-penny per bushel. Steamers even carried wheat oveT as ballast, and brought it back again without waiting to discharge it. In those days, wheat was a drug on the market, and the shipowners were not making very -much money. But now the business has -changed, and the rates are enormously high, largely owing to the war. If you took -an average of ten or fifteen years you would find perhaps that the Government would not make very much money in running the business. The Government never -can run a business as economically and successfully as private enterprise, I am not arguing that the Government should do- nothing. I think they should do something. I think the time has come when this matter ought to be dealt with in some practical -manner. A number of proposals have been made to the minister, and I -think that some of them are practical proposals. What we want to do with the shipowner is to get off his -back, and let him have a fair chance at the business. There -are -too many restric

tions at present. In Canada we have been constantly piling on restrictions. Any one who reads the Canadian Shipping Act will see that they stick out on every page, restrictions in regard to the manning of the ships, to the inspection of the ships, and so on. The great question is the cost of building. It has been stated here tonight, -and i-t is quite true, that the high cost is largely owing to the high tariff we have in this country. When this question was up some years ago, I took the trouble to make some inquiries as to the extra cost of building ships in Canada compared with that of building them in Great Britain. It is true that a -certain number of articles that enter into the construction of a ship were admitted free, the plates, for example, and a few other things; but a large number	of the articles -are
subject to a high protective tariff.
* Some time ago I took the trouble of going to Collingwood to find out how much duty was paid by shipbuilders in that part oi Canada, on the r-aw material entering into *the construction- of a ship. While there I was allowed to look at the books of the largest shipbuilding firm in the town. 1 made an abstract of the figures, and my recollection is that it averaged something like flO on every ton of shipping; a very 
high tax indeed. Many articles imported into this country for use in the construction of a ship are subject to a very high duty. The consequence is that the price of the ship is increased. A proposal that was made at that time was that the duty should be returned to the shipbuilder when he turned out the finished -product. A man who builds ia hinder in this country and sells it in the United States, or any other outside market, gets -a rebate from the customs of ninety-nine per cent of the duty paid on the raw material entering into the binder. The same thing is true with regard to boilers engines, and ail kinds of agricultural machinery. Why should we not apply this principle to ships? When a ship is launched on the sea, it is an export. It has to compete with the whole world for business. If there is a cargo to carry it is chalked up on the blackboard at Lloyds, London, or at some other exchange, and the whole shipping tonnage of the world bids for it. The man who bids the lowest gets the cargo. Now, a man who has to pay $10 a ton more for his ship on account of duty cannot compete for the business. Shipping is like everything else: you have to get a return on your capital. If there is anything that ought to -be regarded as an export it is a completed ship. I think a Canadian-built ship should be treated just as we treat boilers, and binders, and other implements that are made .in this country and exported. This is a practical proposal. It is one which could be carried out, and without injury to anybody. I do not see what possible objection, could be made to it. The question of tonnage is a serious one, and it is going to be more serious as years go by. I do not -see why this matter should not he dealt with at the present session, and I trust the minister will bring the matter before his colleagues and -try and get something done.
The United States has been referred to. Everybody knows that the United States has not been able to build up a mercantile marine, and everybody who thinks about the matter knows that it is in a very large degree due to the high protective tariff. But even the United States has made a move in the direction of building up a mercantile marine. Only last year they struck the tariff off. Here in Canada you cannot buy a ship. If a man wants to puL his capital into the shipping business, he is not' allowed to go -out into the world and buy a ship and register it in this country unless he pays a high protective duty.

Since last July or August, when the new regulations came into effect in the United States, there has been an enormous increase in American tonnage. Since the American Government decided to allow ships to be bought and registered in the United States, under the American flag without the payment of duty, the people of the United States have bought no less than fourteen vessels that were registered in Canada. I understand that at the present time they cannot buy any more Canadian vessels, because our Government have passed an Order in Council prohibiting the sale of Canadian vessels to any foreign country. I think that was a very proper step to take, and I hope the regulation will he kept in effect during the war. At the same time it would not be. a proper regulation to have in force in time of peace.
I have made two practical proposals: one is to put a ship on the same basis as a manufactured article, and allow a rebate on the raw material entering into the ship when it is completed. The other proposal is to strike the duty off and allow the Canadian ship owner to purchase a ship from the markets of the world and register it free of duty under the Canadian flag. The minister knows I have also another little hobby. We have been driving our ships away from Canada. We have actually made them seek refuge in some outside country, because we would not allow them to trade in southern latitudes. The minister will allow them to go as far north as they like. They can go to the rocky coast of Labrador, or to the North Pole in winter time, and the Minister of Marine will make no objection; but when they want to go to the sunny South, amidst the laughing waves and eternal sunshine, the minister says, No, we will not allow you to go. That has been his policy ever since he has been minister.

I should be delighted to
see my hon. friend go South.

As you know, Mr. Chairman, there are numerous ways in which a minister can prevent a private member from securing any reform. It is impossible for a private member to get a bill through this House if the Government do not want the Bill to be passed. Two years ago I introduced a Bill to remedy the disadvantage I have spoken of. The Minister of Marine admitted that I was right. He said that the object of the Bill was good, and referred it to the Committee of Marine and Fisheries. The Committee of Marine and Fisheries never sat, and the Bill died a violent death.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: Not a violent death, a peaceful death.

And I hold the minister responsible for it. Some hon. gentlemen have referred to Great Britain. We all know the two lines of policy that have guided Great Britain-free trade and free ships. The result is that Britain controls one-half of the world's tonnage. The British flag flies in every sea, and Britain does one half of the carrying trade of the world. She could not have done that under a protective system. She could not have done it under our system of charging a duty on ships. There is no necessity in Great Britain for a man to have a coasting license, for everything is free. If a man in Great Britain wants to buy a ship, he can go to the ends of the earth and buy it, and register it under the British flag free of duty. They will welcome it; they are glad to have it.under the British register. Let us adopt a policy like that in Canada, so far as the purchase of ships is concerned. I am not making the proposal that we should abolish the protective tariff in Canada altogether. At this time, when we need money so badly, I do not think it would be practical to strike off all the duties, but we could return to a ship-owner the duty he paid on the raw material entering into his ship. It is only fair that we should do that. These are the practical proposals that I trust the minister will not forget when he takes up this matter with his colleagues.

speakeroldname: Mr. W. F. CARROLL (Cape Breton South):
speechtext:
It seems to me that the two grievances which the business interests of Canada have to-day in this connection are, first, the scarcity of ships, and, secondly, the high rates that shipping companies charge. These difficulties can be surmounted, first of all by building more ships, and, secondly, by having the ships built by interests who will be real rivals to the interests which control shipping in Canada to-day. I may say that the present Prime Minister of Canada, in the course of a speech at Halifax during the election of 1911, did promise some assistance in the building up of a Canadian mercantile marine.	.
I do not think that the right hon. gentle-

One speaker on
the other side stated that there was a tariff on ships imported into this country. There is a tariff on ships imported from foreign countries, but not on ships imported from England, Ireland, or Scotland. Most of the ships imported into Canada are built in Great Britain. Let us look
at this matter in a broad way. It is stated that we can build our own ships. It is possible for us to do so, providing the steel industries will engage in the business of rolling steel. Where does Britain get the * siteel that goes into her ships? I understand that more than half the steel going into ships built in Great Britain before the war was rolled in Belgium and the United States. It is true tha/t this steel goes into that country free of duty.
I think that in this House there are enough men of ability to solve this question. It may be that if the duty were taken off steel, the firm of Vickers Maxim or some other firm in Canada with means could enter into this industry. That is a question that can be solved. It is not necessary to appoint a commission for that purpose. I would suggest to the Government that they get assistance from the men in this House in solving the problem, and that to that end a committee of this House be appointed, composed of business men, to confer on this subject. I do not know whether the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff) and the hon. member for Red Deer" (Mr. Michael Clark) would agree with the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) or the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) in regard to the facts in this case. But I think we ought to attempt this question within the four walls of this House. The Government to-day is engaged in the problem of the present war, and every moment of the time of ministers is taken up with thlse problems. But I think that a great question, such as this, which is engaging the attention of all the business men in this country, should receive the attention of the business men of this House. I have no doubt that members of the Government would take suggestions from the members of this House on this subject. There seems a consensus of opinion that Canada should have ships and should have them at once. We all agree on that. How can we obtain these ships as cheaply as they are built in Great Britain? That question the Government can solve, I believe, with the House. There would be no harm in making a trial by appointing a committee. We may not all agree, but let us set aside our politics for a time and see if we cannot deal with this grave and important question. It is a question for this Parliament to solve. What are we here for? We are here to do the business of the people of this country, and this question of ship-

I have listened with great interest to this discussion, for shipbuilding is a matter that has engaged my attention for three or four years. If anything were necessary to bring home to me the difficulty of the problem, I think it would'be found in the speeches of the hon. member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Carroll), thp hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Turriff), and the hon. member for Guys-borough (Mr. Sinclair). The hon. member for Assiniboia comes from a rural district where grain is the chief product, and with characteristic shrewdness he sees that if the cost of a ship is increased, the cost of transporting grain by that ship must pe increased. And, as the price of the article of export is fixed in the foreign market, when the cost of transportation is increased, the return to the producer must be lessened. Therefore, he says: Let us have free trade in all that goes into the making of a ship, because in that way you will lessen the cost of transportation. The hon. member for Guysborough comes from the East. He is not particularly concerned about the cost of transportation, but would like to see shipping developed on the seaboard. Therefore, he says: Let us take the duty off. ships, and let the ships of all countries come into this country free of duty; in that way you will build up a great marine. But the hon. member for South Cape Breton sees that if the duty is taken off steel, a great business in his constituency will suffer. Therefore he says: Do not take the duty off steel; leave the duty on the component parts of the ship; develop the steel industry in Canada, pay 
the builders a bounty and we shall have a great mercantile marine. Let us face the question fairly and squarely. England has developed a great manufacture of ships. Three things have contributed to her success in this matter. She has coal, she has steel, and she has cheap labour. So her vessels cover the seven seas, and she controls the shipping of the world. The hon. member for Guysborough says: Let us rebate to the manufacturer of ships whatever duty the Government collects on the commodities that enter into the composition of the ship. Now, I have given this matter some thought, and know whereof I speak when I say that this would not solve the problem in its entirety. Two factors enter into the cost of an article-the material and the labour. If you were to rebate to the manufacturer every dollar he had paid in duty, he would still be at a disadvantage, comparing the wages paid to the skilled mechanic here with those paid in England. Further, in a highly organized manufacturing industry such as shipbuilding, the Canadian manufacturer is at a disadvantage because the overhead charges per dollar of production are infinitely greater than in the very highly organized and efficient plants that they have in England.
You have to go farther than rebate to the Canadian manufacturer the duty that he pays on the article. You have to develop some scheme by which the difference in wages ,is met. It would be manifestly unfair to ask the steel worker in this country to take a wage that would not bring him an adequate return for his labour. If you attempted such a thing the inevitable result would be that he would turn bis attention to some other means of earning a livelihood. That leaves you but one other way to manage the situation, and I quite agree with what hon. members on this and the other side have said that the Government should face "this shipbuilding problem. I see no way of doing it unless you can develop some system by which a certain tonnage bounty is going to be given. There is a small subsidy paid, so small that it does not amount to much. But on taking this matter into consideration, there are three things that you have to keep in view. You have to keep in view the fact that the farmer of the West will not stand an increased freight Tate, because that lessens the profit on his product; you have to take into consideration, in the second place, the fast that the skilled artisan is

not going to take a small wage to develop a national industry, and you have to take into consideration that if Canada wants a shipbuilding industry established, the entire people must bear a part of the burden during the pexiod while that industry is in its development stage.

I do not mind, but I do not like to hear the statement made that this work was done by contract. I do not think it was.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext:
That is the information
given me by the officers of my department and my deputy minister says that he is satisfied that it is correct. However, I will get the information.
What is the rule about the removal of these wrecks? I understood that the owner of the vessel had to remove a wreck at his own expense.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: That is the rule. If there is a wreck, we ascertain who are the owners of the vessel and we give them notice to remove the wreck. Some times they do it and there is no further trouble, but in other cases they do not do it promptly and we have to do it and then we endeavour to collect from the owners. In some cases we succeed in collecting, but in some cases these vessels are owned by people who are really not worth anything and we do not succeed. But, the rule is that we notify the person to remove the wreck and if he does not we do it, charge the cost to him and endeavour to collect it.
I have something to say about the next item, for "winter mail service," and as it is now eleven o'clock, I think we might leave it for another time.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is for the winter service between Cape Tormentine and Cape Traverse by the ice boats. Is that the item that my hon. friend wishes me to discuss?
I think we have got along very well, and it is rather late. I assume that is the general vote for that purpose?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: This is for the service between Cape Traverse and Cape Tormentine when you have to cross by open boat. There are times when no steamer can cross and there is a crossing at the capes.
I do not think the minister would lose anything by adjourning, because my hon. friend would like to discuss that matter.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: I am not objecting, but I did not suppose that that was the item that my hon. friend desired to discuss.

What I have to say will be very much on the general question.
